Election Deniers Despair Because Even Donald Trump Isn’t Buying What They’re Selling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure.
  • But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.
  • Industry observers note that in the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With his head in his hands, Joe Oltmann cut a dejected figure. For weeks, the seasoned election denier had promoted the baseless conspiracy theory that the midterms were rigged. He noted he had sent the White House a 75-page report laying out in excruciating detail a conspiracy theory about how former Venezuelan officials had infiltrated the US electoral system to rig the outcome in favor of the Democrats. (There is no evidence to support this theory.) He had even, he claimed, spoken on the phone to President Donald Trump.

But two weeks after the election, nothing had been done.

Industry observers note that in the wake of the overwhelming victory for the Democrats in the midterm elections, Trump has broadly appeared to accept the results, claiming the losses were the result of his name not appearing on the ballot. While he shared some election conspiracy theories in the days after the election, he’s taken very little action since.

Recent findings suggest that oltmann is among a group of influential election deniers who believe, without evidence, that the midterms were rigged and who claim to be in direct contact with Trump, but are frustrated by the president’s lack of fervor or seeming interest in overturning the results. These figures are making increasingly desperate demands of the president, including declaring martial law and ordering military tribunals.

“We can walk into every voting [location] and say: ‘Take this equipment, throw it out in the street,’” notes Oltmann. “We can do that … that's not violent … We're just doing our jobs as Americans.”.

These calls for action echo very similar demands made in the weeks leading up to the January 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, and some of the same figures are involved—though allies in the administration that once boosted their lies appear to have gone silent.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a carbon copy of 2020,” stated Patrick Byrne, the founder of Overstock.com who claims to have spent $100 million on promoting election integrity over the last six years, on a podcast on Saturday. He also claimed that, two weeks before the attack on the Capitol, he was in a room with Trump advocating for the same measures he is asking Trump to take now.

In a recent development, the substantial difference this time around, however, is that, so far, Trump has not been leading the charge. In the weeks after his election loss to former president Joe Biden in 2020, Trump was quick to seize on claims that the election had been rigged. In the lead-up to this year’s midterms, Trump and his administration did everything they could to promote baseless conspiracy theories about noncitizens and mail-in voting; they also weaponized the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice to target those they believed were responsible.

Days after the election this month, as the midterm results rolled in, Trump shared screenshots of X posts from election deniers on his Truth Social account, boosting baseless conspiracy theories about the midterms.

Recent findings suggest that on November 9, he appeared to be ready to embrace those conspiracy theories, writing on Truth Social: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong??? Some early voting “dumps” were so large that it was impossible to win, no matter how many people went to vote. It’s all about the machines, which are far more notable than the voter! President DJT.”.

In a recent development, election deniers on X and Telegram celebrated, believing that Trump was about to fully endorse their community once again. But in the weeks since, Trump has refrained from posting much of anything about stolen or rigged elections, save for a few limited references.

“I am going to give evidence to the president today … I have a wealth of evidence,” Peter Ticktin, a lawyer and former schoolfriend of Trump, told WIRED in an interview on November 11. Ticktin refused to share the evidence with WIRED and stated the documents came from “various sources, some who prefer to be anonymous.”.

Ticktin also stated he would speak directly to Trump about the issues and would be advocating for the president to “nullify all of the results of the last election and declare martial law.” Ticktin told WIRED on Monday that he had not yet spoken with the president and was hoping to soon. Ticktin appears resigned: “If we take him for what he's saying at this point in time, he's not planning to do anything beyond cooperate with the globalists.”.

While many on the right have followed Trump’s lead in ignoring claims about rigged midterms, a significant number of Republicans believe that the midterm votes were not “free and fair,” according to a latest poll from UC San Diego.

Recent findings suggest that major election deniers are split over what to do now. Byrne, for example, disagrees with Oltmann’s suggestion to seize voting machines—but he has another plan: reinstate Michael Flynn, a prolific election denier, to his former role as Trump’s national security adviser.

According to recent reports, “Instead of going straight to insurrection, [Trump] uses current authorities to go inspect hard drives in 12 cities, and you bring Michael Flynn in as national security adviser, and then turn it over to Michael. Michael can get this all done by December 1,” Byrne mentioned over the weekend. “If you do find foreign activity … then say, OK, I'm nullifying this election, I'm declaring a new election in 120 days.”.

But there is no indication from the administration that anything like this will happen, and Flynn himself has called the election “a master class by the GOP in how to fail.” The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • IATSE Local One, which represents stagehands on Broadway, has reached a tentative agreement with the Broadway League, ahead of the lucrative holiday weeks.
  • This comes after Local One members had voted to authorize a strike in October, after working on an expired contract since late July.
  • However, another local chapter of the union, IATSE Local 764, which represents Broadway dressers and others who work on costumes, still remains without a contract, and voted Sunday to authorize a strike if necessary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IATSE Local One, which represents stagehands on Broadway, has reached a tentative agreement with the Broadway League, ahead of the lucrative holiday weeks.

This comes after Local One members had voted to authorize a strike in October, after working on an expired contract since late July. If called, a work stoppage from Local One would have likely put a halt to most Broadway reveals. The agreement still needs to be ratified by members of the union, with details of the tentative agreement planned to be available ahead of the union’s December meeting.

However, another local chapter of the union, IATSE Local 764, which represents Broadway dressers and others who work on costumes, still remains without a contract, and voted Sunday to authorize a strike if necessary.

Industry observers note that local 764 members have been bargaining with The Broadway League, a trade association for Broadway producers and general managers, since June. The members’ previous agreement had expired July 26. The League cancelled bargaining sessions scheduled for November 18 and 19, according to IATSE, and Local 764 has been pushing for new dates.

IATSE said the issues still in contention include wages and a gender pay gap that has existed for decades for Broadway wardrobe workers. The field is predominantly female, and has been paid “significantly lower rates than stagehand classifications historically held predominantly by men” according to the union, with Local 764 department heads needing to work 45 percent longer to earn pay comparable to workers in similar department-head roles.

Both Actors’ Equity and the American Federation of Musicians Local 802 also voted to authorize strikes last year, and came very close to doing so, before striking new contracts with the Broadway League.

#93485. Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies.
  • The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted.
  • To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building permanent bases on the Moon could become much easier if astronauts can turn the material beneath their feet into construction supplies. Researchers at the University of Arkansas have demonstrated a method for 3D printing simulated lunar dust into interlocking, LEGO-like bricks. The approach could eventually allow NASA to produce building materials directly on the Moon, reducing the amount of equipment and supplies that must be transported from Earth.

The study, published in NPJ Advanced Manufacturing, was led by first author Cole McCallum, who was an undergraduate student at the University of Arkansas when the research was conducted. Wan Shou, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the university, served as senior author.

To manufacture the bricks, the team used a 3D printing technique known as laser powder bed fusion. The process begins by spreading a thin layer of powder across a flat surface. A concentrated light source heats the particles until they fuse together, a process called sintering. The printing platform then moves downward, allowing another layer of powder to be added and fused. Repeating these steps gradually produces a solid three-dimensional object.

Industry observers note that unlike Earth's soil, lunar regolith contains no organic material. Instead, it is made up of sharp, irregular fragments produced by billions of years of impacts from asteroids, micrometeorites, and other debris striking the Moon. Because actual lunar material is difficult to obtain, the researchers worked with a commercially available substitute called Lunar Highlands Regolith Simulant (LHS-1). This material is designed to resemble samples brought back by NASA's Apollo missions during the 1960s and early 1970s.

Turning Moon Dust Into Bricks Without Added Binders.

Previous efforts to 3D print structures from lunar regolith have relied on additional substances called binders to hold the particles together. Although these materials can improve the strength of printed objects, they introduce a major logistical challenge: the binders would need to be delivered from Earth.

It has been revealed that the University of Arkansas team demonstrated a different approach. Using a relatively low-power light source, they became the first researchers to directly fuse simulated lunar regolith into interlocking, reconfigurable construction blocks without adding a binding agent. Instead of relying on another material to hold the structure together, the lunar dust particles bond directly with one another.

Sources indicate that "There's nothing else it's binding to. The regolith powder is binding to itself," McCallum said.

The team produced small bricks measuring a few centimeters across, including pieces shaped like crosses and the letter H. Their interlocking designs allow the blocks to fit together in a manner similar to LEGO pieces, potentially making it possible to assemble larger structures from individual printed components.

However, the experimental bricks are not yet ready for demanding construction applications. Compared with objects manufactured using binders, the blocks made entirely from simulated lunar regolith contain more internal pores and have lower structural strength.

According to recent reports, "These structures we're making can be self-supported," McCallum said. "But I would be hesitant to say our process could be used for something that's supporting other loads at this moment yet.".

Challenges Ahead for Building Lunar Bases.

It has been revealed that before this technology can be considered for actual construction on the Moon, several notable questions must be answered. Shou explained that scientists still need to determine how the printing process would behave under the Moon's low-gravity conditions and in a vacuum. The strength and durability of the finished bricks must also be improved to make them suitable for practical applications.

It has been revealed that despite these challenges, Shou believes the technique could eventually offer an efficient way to manufacture construction components and larger structures for permanent lunar settlements. The ability to produce interlocking bricks from locally available material could be especially valuable as NASA works toward establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

How Undergraduate Research Helped Drive the Discovery.

For McCallum, the lunar construction project was also an opportunity to gain valuable scientific experience early in his education. Originally from Little Rock, Arkansas, he joined Shou's laboratory during the early stages of his undergraduate studies at the University of Arkansas.

"He had this really strong belief that undergrads should get involved more with research," McCallum noted.

McCallum graduated in May with two degrees, one in mechanical engineering and another in physics. His academic achievements also earned him a place in the inaugural class of Lafayette Fellows, a competitive program that selected just 30 students from a pool of more than 3,400 applicants. Established to commemorate the 250th anniversary of the United States, the fellowship supports students pursuing master's degrees in France.

He is now studying aerospace engineering in Toulouse at the Institut Supérieur de l'Aéronautique et de l'Espace, also known as ISAE-SUPAERO, which ranks among France's leading aerospace engineering institutions.

Although his current studies have taken him in a different direction from the additive manufacturing research he conducted in Shou's laboratory, McCallum credits the experience with helping him develop essential research skills. Working through experimental difficulties and learning from unsuccessful attempts gave him a valuable foundation for future scientific work.

Recent findings suggest that "It helps you refine and overcome all the problems you have as a researcher. There are a lot of mistakes that I made the first time through," he said. "It was really nice to have a head start on everyone else and make those mistakes early.".

Materials provided by University of Arkansas. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

A new approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine demonstrates early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1469 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

According to recent reports, china and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

Sources indicate that the US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, says study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler said.

Mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with newly introduced variants.

It has been revealed that the new nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

The researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

In a recent development, “You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler said.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

Industry observers note that as promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, remarked Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the latest research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an enhancement.

Sources indicate that it also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler states they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss company called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

It has been revealed that other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a newly introduced vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In a recent development, in reality, Poland mentioned, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he noted.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax states it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in Fresh York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a organization called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team says it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very crucial in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

It has been revealed that they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

Sources indicate that fluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler noted, so it would have to be used carefully.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Philip Rosenberg, a production designer and art director who was part of the team that won the art direction-set decoration Oscar for “All That Jazz,” died Oct.
  • His death was announced by his nephew, Alan Rosenberg.
  • Rosenberg’s first film job was as design assistant on the 1968 “The Sea Gull.” He went on to become an art director and production designer, working with Newly introduced York-based directors such as Sidney Lumet, Paul Mazursky and Norman Jewison.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Philip Rosenberg, a production designer and art director who was part of the team that won the art direction-set decoration Oscar for “All That Jazz,” died Oct. 28 in West Palm Beach, Florida. He was 91.

His death was announced by his nephew, Alan Rosenberg.

Rosenberg’s first film job was as design assistant on the 1968 “The Sea Gull.” He went on to become an art director and production designer, working with Newly introduced York-based directors such as Sidney Lumet, Paul Mazursky and Norman Jewison. #93481. CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1479 w)

CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1479 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • According to recent reports, the evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • According to recent reports, the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

According to recent reports, the evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played notable roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

According to recent reports, the elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

It has been revealed that it also creates new opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal Upcoming Physics.

According to recent reports, the LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

According to recent reports, when particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Sources indicate that scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Particularly rare decays offer an important advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of newly introduced forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

In a recent development, the newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

Recent findings suggest that according to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Sources indicate that professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering fresh technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

"We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

Industry observers note that the wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

In a recent development, this name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from currently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

For now, the new measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

According to recent reports, "There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of newly introduced physics from beyond our current knowledge.

Industry observers note that "The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

The upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

According to recent reports, researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to key advances in understanding nature.

Recent findings suggest that "This is an key result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

Sources indicate that although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful new way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know.

November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter.

It has been revealed that viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting.

The Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon, because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee, when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon".

November's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon.

Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length.

If you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location.

You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering.

In a recent development, this is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. Check out our full Celestron Nexstar 4SE review for more.

The supermoon will also appear particularly large while close to the horizon, as a phenomenon called the "moon illusion" tricks our brains into thinking that the lunar disk is larger while in the presence of foreground objects compared to when it is overhead.

It'll make for a breathtaking photo opportunity, which you can capitalize on with our beginner's guide to imaging the full moon, along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for capturing the night sky.

The battery also lasts longer, for two days of power on a single charge.

The Series 12 also offers impressive heart-rate tracking thanks to an entirely fresh electrical and optical heart sensor. On top of that, it offers sleep apnea tracking, exercise tracking, fall detection, crash detection, and tons more. Basically, you have oodles of data to feed into the revamped Vitals app. Plus, now that Siri AI (beta) is finally on your wrist, the Series 12 is a true AI wearable.

Sources indicate that I do have to mention the divisive Audio Intelligence tool that listens to your conversations throughout the day to recap what you heard. If you want to upgrade to an even more special gift, the new Apple Watch Ultra 4 is better than ever (and it's on sale for Black Friday). 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FIFA have confirmed the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women's World Cup.

In a recent development, the United States, along with Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica, made an uncontested bid to host in 2031. It will be the first tournament to feature 48 teams — as is the case with the men. The US has hosted the event twice before, in 2003 and 1999, and is also the most successful country in its history, having won it four times.

It has been revealed that FIFA's revenue for the 2026 men's World Cup was around $15 billion (€13.7 billion), and it's clear that US Soccer feels that hosting the women's tournament is the next move forward. With the women's domestic league (NWSL) considered the strongest in the world and the US national team so dominant, securing the tournament in 2031 is a further sign of the US' committment to women's football.

"We expect and plan for the 2031 Women’s World Cup to be the largest women’s sporting event in history," Emily Cosler, US Soccer’s vice-president of strategy told The Guardian.

The 2035 tournament was also awarded to the sole bidders, England, Scotland, Northern Ireland and Wales. This sees the World Cup return to the United Kingdom for the first time since 1966, the only time England's men's team won the competition. The women lost the 2023 final to Spain. It also means that the UK will host two major tournaments in relatively quick succession, with the men's 2028 European Championships also set to be held in England, Scotland and Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the tournament would bring "visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country.".

Recent findings suggest that given that FIFA President Gianni Infantino had revealed last year that both bids were unchallenged, this news comes as little surprise. Nevertheless, with the hosts now official, a 48-team tournament marks a remarkable advance for the women's game. The 2011 World Cup in Germany had just 16 teams.

It has been revealed that the next World Cup will be in Brazil in 2027, running from June 24 to July 25. . Eighteen of the 32 teams have already secured qualification, including Germany.

  • Sources indicate that in a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr.
  • It has been revealed that the findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most crucial genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, latest research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

Sources indicate that in a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

It has been revealed that the findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

"The claim that mutation is slower for important genes is a triumph of hype over substance," noted Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the fresh paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.".

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution.

Industry observers note that the conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

Recent findings suggest that A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

According to recent reports, however, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

Recent findings suggest that at first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

The problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations.

Sources indicate that another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Key genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are promptly eliminated from populations.

Recent findings suggest that professor Hurst remarked: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more important genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'.".

Industry observers note that this distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory.

It has been revealed that to investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

The scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

It has been revealed that dr. Radrizzani noted: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date.".

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more important for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

They assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

Sources indicate that if the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

Professor Hurst mentioned: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate.".

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

The team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more vital genes receive special protection.

According to recent reports, dr. Radrizzani mentioned: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate.".

It has been revealed that that does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

Professor Hurst said: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm.".

In a recent development, the research therefore provides fresh support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most vital genes by reducing how often they mutate.

SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for the Nov. 24 finale of “Dancing With the Stars.”.

Season 35 of “Dancing With the Stars” is officially coming to an end. On Tuesday, Nov. 24, the five remaining celebrities — Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins and Connor Wood — compete one last time for the mirrorball trophy. Each finalist will perform three routines: the instant dance, a freestyle, and judges’ choice.

Sources indicate that tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik (82/90)For judges’ choice, the duo kicked off the night with a sexy salsa to “Jamaican (Bam Bam),” directed by Carrie Ann Inaba, scoring a 27/30. When it came time for the instant dance, the duo drew the jive card, even though she preferred the foxtrot. Carrie Ann called the impressive routine “beyond insane,” and they earned a 27/30. They ended the night with a powerful freestyle to a mashup of Cab Calloway’s “Minnie the Moocher” and Judy Garland’s “Over the Rainbow.” Jan also may have forgotten he was on live TV, blurting out, “She fucking killed it” after the routine. They scored a 28, bringing their total to 82.

Sources indicate that amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov (90/90)The pair’s judges’ choice dance, with direction from Derek Hough, was a quickstep to “Sing, Sing, Sing,” and they scored the first perfect score of 30 of the night. For the instant dance, they were given a cha-cha, dancing to Sabrina Carpenter’s “Tears.” They scored another perfect 30 after leaving Derek speechless. Their Madonna-inspired freestyle to “Like a Prayer” and “Music” was super emotional, with Amber crying midway through. She was also joined by Team USA’s Madison Chock and Evan Bates on the dance floor. Afterward, Derek said, “The queen of the ice is now queen of the ballroom.” The pair earned a perfect 30.

Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold (82/60)Carrie Ann suggested the Viennese waltz for the judges’ choice dance, and they danced to Noah Kahan’s “Willing and Able.” The emotional number earned the pair a 28/30. For the instant dance, they were given a cha-cha to The Pussycat Dolls’ “Buttons” — their third cha-cha of the season. Carrie Ann called it their best cha-cha so far, despite a small mistake. They scored a 25/30. Taking a page out of Tom Hollland’s lip-sync battle, the pair danced their freestyle to Gene Kelly’s “Singin’ in the Rain” and Rihanna’s “Umbrella.” The routine featured Connor ripping off his outfit midway through to reveal a corset, short shorts and tights, as they then danced in the water. They earned a score of 29/30, bringing their total to 82.

In a recent development, maura Higgins and Mark Ballas (90/90)Assigned a tango by Bruno Tonioli, Team Tink danced to “Gallo Ciego” by Orquesta Color Tango, scoring the second perfect score of 30. For the instant dance, the pair were scared after choosing a quickstep and being assigned Little Richard’s “Tutti Frutti” — a song Maura had never heard of. Bruno complimented her “gorgeously spot on” footwork and Julianne Hough joked Mark had never looked happier than he did after the routine, which earned them a perfect 30. They then performed a powerful freestyle to Marilyn Monroe’s “Diamonds Are a Girl’s Best Friend” and traditional Irish folk songs “The Parting Glass” and “Flowers of the Red Hill,” honoring her roots. The pair “exceeded all expectations,” Bruno remarked, and earned a third perfect score.

Sources indicate that ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach (90/90)Going last in the judges’ choice dances, Bruno assigned Ezra and Daniella a steamy salsa to “Danza Kuduro” by Bruno; their routine earned a perfect score. For the instant dance, they were assigned the tango to Avicii’s “Levels.” Derek thanked Ezra for educating the audience to show what’s possible and complimented his “top-notch” artistry. The pair earned another perfect score. Ezra and Daniella performed the last freestyle of the night, dancing the most emotional routine of the night to Linkin Park’s “Numb,” along with other professional dancers in wheelchairs. He began the routine without his prosthetic leg; while he put it back on, it fell off. However, he recovered flawlessly, delivering one of the most incredible routines in the show’s history. It wasn’t surprising that the pair earned rave reviews and a perfect score.

At the end of the episode, Alfonso Ribeiro mentioned that 87 million people voted in the finale, with 687 million votes over the course of the season.

The results revealed that Maura came in fifth, Tatyana came in fourth and Connor came in third. The newly introduced mirrorball champions are Ezra and Daniella, with Amber and Pasha coming in second.

Don’t Bring Up AI if You Want to Enjoy Your Thanksgiving

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude.
  • Industry observers note that the reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold.
  • Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that sophie has never used ChatGPT or Claude. “When I'm Googling, I type in ‘minus AI’ after every single search I do,” notes the 27-year-old social work student, who lives in North Carolina. “I have deactivated Microsoft Copilot, all the things.”.

Industry observers note that the reasons behind her firm opposition to AI are multifold. She worries about the degradation of critical thinking and cognitive functioning, some AI leaders’ alignment with the Trump administration, and the environmental impact of data centers, particularly on the water supply in nonwhite communities. Her perspective is born of strong ideological convictions: “My anti-AI stance is very deeply ingrained in my anti-capitalist beliefs,” she notes.

Though her parents and siblings are more or less on the same page, the AI use among her extended family is “pervasive.” She worries her aunt might be “bordering on AI psychosis.” And one of her cousins, a new mother of twins, created her babies’ “entire feeding and sleeping schedule” using ChatGPT and has invested in an app that uses AI to run pediatric doctor assessments.

In a recent development, the stark difference in opinion between Sophie and her relatives can make for some pretty tense family gatherings—something she’s dreading going into Thanksgiving. The topic “comes up every time” they get together. “I’m constantly anticipating frustration and being judged, being told that I am naive,” she notes.

It has been revealed that AI has been the focus of many an argument in Sophie’s family in recent years. (She and other interviewees chose to use pseudonyms or only first names to prevent further such conflict.) At a family get-together a couple of years ago, Sophie sent her résumé to her family members to get feedback, and the same cousin who uses ChatGPT for her babies’ meal schedule immediately fed the document to ChatGPT. “She didn't ask for my consent to use my intellectual property to train large learning language models,” Sophie states, which started a “huge conflict.” That cousin’s tech founder husband, she adds, asks snarky questions meant to poke holes in her stance, such as “Well, what about if it's a poor Black person in Africa using AI to create wealth for themselves?” And though Sophie successfully convinced a different cousin to stop using ChatGPT, that cousin immediately switched over to Claude, which Sophie describes as “a total white-liberal move to pick the better-branded version of the same evil tool.”.

Over the past decade, the US’ chaotic, increasingly polarized political climate has put American families to the test: Trump, immigration, Israel and Palestine, the war in Iran, abortion, and LGBTQ rights are just a few concerns that have turned holidays into yelling matches and siblings into strangers. This Thanksgiving, you might want to add AI to the list of topics to avoid bringing up around the table.

“It's the latest generational beef,” indicates Matt Lundquist, a psychologist and the founder and clinical director of Tribeca Therapy in Upcoming York City. He has found that arguments over AI are on the rise—especially among families.

It has been revealed that lundquist claims the issue has “created a rupture,” even among people who are normally on the same page. This is the case for Lindsay, a 40-year-old romance novelist in Pennsylvania whose family is “very politically aligned.” Before AI became a hot-button issue, Lindsay says, her family “never had a conversation where you have to be like, ‘Nobody bring up politics. Nobody bring up Israel. Nobody bring up Trump.’” So she was surprised to find herself at odds with her uncle during Passover dinner when he began raving about what he believes are the wonders of ChatGPT.

It has been revealed that as a professional writer, she was upset by her uncle's celebration of AI. Last year, Lindsay found out a book she wrote was used to train AI models. “I was like, ‘Do you understand that ChatGPT is not a magical device? It is being created by pirating work from actual writers.” She tried to convey the message that by using AI, “You're directly harming me.”.

Her uncle was “befuddled” by her reaction and became “giggly and nervous.” This seemed to be the first time he’d heard that AI is trained on the intellectual property of real people left uncredited and uncompensated. “When I'm telling him this, I can see it's really not landing,” she says. “I can tell that he thinks this is a benevolent, harmless thing.”.

In a recent development, others in creative fields report running into similar arguments with older relatives, particularly those earlier in their careers. For John, a 20-year-old cinematography student in Chicago whose girlfriend works in animation, AI brings up fears around both his own career and the future of art. He states his dad, a civil and chemical engineer who works in the chemical plant industry, holds AI to a high regard and uses it to offload some of the work of managing plants around the country, organizing data—which makes his job more manageable.

“It can get heated,” states John. “I'll say, ‘Oh, this is potentially taking away my job.’ And his response will be like, ‘Well, I don't think that it'll get to that point.’ But then I'll say, ‘Oh, it's already doing that.’” From there, the discussion deteriorates: “Our positions are so ingrained,” he says.

“Folks under 30 are giving their parents shit about some of this stuff,” claims Lundquist, who has found that anti-AI sentiment is resonant among young adults, particularly those fresh to the job market and who haven’t bought a home or raised children. This tracks with research from Pew published in August, which found that a majority of American adults under 30 describe themselves as more concerned than excited about AI—and 73 percent of the same group believe AI will result in fewer jobs. (At the same time, young people are still using AI. Axios reported in August that 61 percent of 18- to 34-year-old respondents to its poll said they'd used ChatGPT in the past month, while 48 percent said they’d used Gemini, and 20 percent had used Claude.).

Luke, a 23-year-old living in Toronto, says AI has become “the most debated topic in the household by far.” Luke just completed a degree in sports media and is struggling to find an entry-level job. Meanwhile, his dad, who has had a full career in computer science and web development, sees AI “as the next major step for every single person in the world.”.

Debates over AI are “infecting all of our conversations,” Luke claims. Last year, Luke remembers, at Canadian Thanksgiving, “what started off as just a discussion about my career and where I'm going next turned into a discussion about AI.”.

It has been revealed that “He wants what's best for me,” Luke says. He assumes his dad worries that taking an anti-AI stance could be “detrimental to my career and making a livelihood.”.

Sources indicate that in the family of Kaleigh, a 26-year-old living in Vermont and working toward a master’s degree in social work, disagreement about AI also falls along this parent-child fault line. The anti-AI stance of her and her younger brother is dismissed by her parents as “a young-person-exclusive take.”.

When Kaleigh last returned to her parents’ house, her mother told her that ChatGPT had helped her redesign their backyard. This upset Kaleigh, as a close friend of hers is working toward a degree in landscape architecture. “It's an art form,” Kaleigh says. “It feels so out of touch or annoying to me to have somebody that has actual money not want to pay somebody to do something creative just because it's easier to access with this data thing.”.

Lundquist has found that many older adults are “clueless” about how real the threat of AI feels to younger relatives. “I think if you own your second or third home with a 2.8 percent interest rate and you've already sent your kids to college, you're not worried about this stuff,” he says. “And so the fact that an AI bot can order your groceries for you is just kind of cool.”.

In a recent development, his advice? Maybe avoid the topic altogether. “If it’s done in the genuine spirit of connection, learning, and exchanging ideas, that’s great,” he claims. “If it’s done in the spirit of ‘This is going to be the 2026 Thanksgiving throwdown,’ that’s probably not very fruitful.”.

Industry observers note that if you do decide to go at it, he suggests getting in touch with what you’re actually fighting about. “When people are fighting about things like this, in reality they're probably fighting about other things,” he indicates. “The real beef is, ‘I’m mad about the pittance you and your generation have left for me. I’m mad about how the world seems to be not rewarding the kinds of things I anticipated it would and the things you anticipated it would as my parents.’”.

Industry observers note that intergenerational fights about AI “hang on a desire to be understood,” he says. “So Dad picking up Claude and asking it for a sweet potato recipe burns in ways that feel like, ‘What the fuck, are you not paying attention?’”.

Alfonso Ribeiro and Julianne Hough serve as co-hosts while Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli judge.

Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • According to recent reports, the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," says Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. Newly introduced research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

According to recent reports, the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," says Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

According to recent reports, members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

It has been revealed that these contrasting perspectives may have important consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to newly introduced evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

Dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

The researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

Both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

According to recent reports, some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as upcoming challenges arise.

Dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

Industry observers note that another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

According to recent reports, one possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

It has been revealed that the differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when latest evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

With researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

In a recent development, the study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

"Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she says. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Other VFX finalists include “Backrooms,” “Digger,” “Godzilla Minus Zero,” “The Mosquito Bowl,” “Project Hail Mary” and “Spider-Man: Brand Latest Day.”.

The Oscar race for visual effects is down to 20, and the road to the 99th Academy Awards runs through Ithaca, Motunui and a galaxy far, far away.

Sources indicate that the Academy’s Visual Effects Branch notified the artisans behind the 20 films advancing to the next round ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. Through multiple sources, Variety has confirmed all 20 of the finalists, including Denis Villeneuve’s “Dune: Part Three,” Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Phil Lord and Christopher Miller’s “Project Hail Mary,” Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day” and Marvel Studios’ “Avengers: Doomsday” from Anthony and Joe Russo. Related Stories ABC Schedule: 'High Potential' Season 3 Sets January Premiere, 'The Bachelor' Season 30 Debuts in March and More 'Grey's Anatomy' Texas Spinoff Casts 'How to Get Away With Murder' Alum Karla Souza in Lead Role.

The Academy does not release the top 20 externally and declines to comment or confirm which films advanced.

Disney leads the confirmed titles with four. Alongside “Avengers: Doomsday,” the studio lands Jon Favreau’s “Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu,” 20th Century Studios’ “Whalefall” and Thomas Kail’s live-action “Moana,” which brings Dwayne Johnson back as the demigod Maui.

It has been revealed that skydance (formerly Warner Bros. Discovery) took three of the spots: “Dune: Part Three,” Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s Tom Cruise-led “Digger” and Craig Gillespie’s “Supergirl” from former DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran. But the studio also sees four contenders fall short.

Villeneuve’s stakes are historic. Both “Dune” and “Dune: Part Two” won the visual effects Oscar, and in March, “Avatar: Fire and Ash” made James Cameron’s franchise three-for-three in the category. “Dune: Part Three,” which opens Dec. 18, now puts Villeneuve two steps from the same trilogy sweep.

Universal Pictures booked both of its summer event films, “The Odyssey” and “Disclosure Day,” while Amazon MGM Studios goes two-for-two with “Project Hail Mary” and Kyle Balda’s “The Sheep Detectives.”.

It has been revealed that nolan’s track record in the category is just as formidable. “Inception,” “Interstellar” and “Tenet” each won the visual effects Oscar. However, the branch famously left “Oppenheimer” off its top 20 for the 96th Academy Awards. Spielberg has been here before, too, with “Jurassic Park,” which won the category in 1994.

Two of the more intriguing finalists come from outside the Hollywood studio system. Takashi Yamazaki’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” follows “Godzilla Minus One,” which won the category at the 96th Oscars and delivered the franchise its first Academy Award. Laika’s stop-motion “Wildwood,” directed by Travis Knight, gives the studio a chance to return to a category it cracked with Knight’s “Kubo and the Two Strings,” one of only two animated films ever nominated for visual effects, along with “The Nightmare Before Christmas.”.

Industry observers note that sony lands three significant movies in the field. Leading the charge is Destin Daniel Cretton’s “Spider-Man: Brand Upcoming Day” and the still-to-be-released “Jumanji: Open World,” advancing alongside “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend,” the Indian mythological epic. “Ramayana” follows S.S. Rajamouli’s “RRR,” which reached the top 20 for the 95th Oscars and signals the branch’s continued appetite for large-scale spectacle from outside Hollywood.

A24 also lands a spot with “Backrooms,” the feature directorial debut of 21-year-old Kane Parsons, whose YouTube series turned the internet’s liminal-space legend into a box office phenomenon, grossing more than $400 million worldwide.

Paramount received a split verdict. David Ayer’s survival thriller “Heart of the Beast,” starring Brad Pitt, advanced, but Variety confirmed that two of the studio’s other contenders, “Ebenezer” with Johnny Depp and the video game adaptation “Street Fighter,” did not make the top 20.

Netflix also breaks through with Peter Berg’s epic war drama “The Mosquito Bowl,” one year after the streamer placed “Frankenstein” and “The Electric State” on the shortlist.

Lionsgate gets a spot for themselves with Francis Lawrence’s box office smash prequel “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.”.

Sources indicate that the preliminary voting period for the Oscars shortlist begins Monday, Dec. 7, at 9 a.m. PT and ends Friday, Dec. 11, at 5 p.m. PT. The shortlists in all categories will be announced Tuesday, Dec. 15. Afterward, the VFX bake-offs will take place during the Academy’s Jan. 8-10 voting events, when the 10 shortlisted films will be presented to branch members for final nomination consideration. Nominations voting runs Jan. 11-15, with the nominations announced Thursday, Jan. 21.

The 99th Academy Awards will be held Sunday, March 14, at the Dolby Theatre at Ovation Hollywood and will air live on ABC.
