📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disney on Tuesday reported quarterly earnings and revenue that exceeded analysts' expectations and unveiled it's targeting $3 billion in cost savings by fiscal 2029.

Recent findings suggest that those cost-cutting efforts include several rounds of layoffs announced in recent months, Disney's chief financial officer, Hugh Johnston, told CNBC. The most recent round, which seeks to reduce costs by up to 20%, was reported earlier this month.

Future cost-saving measures will include reductions in administrative and other general expenses, Johnston said, while adding, "We do expect more layoffs.".

Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro told investors on the company's earnings call that the job cuts are "not easy.".

"They affect people who care deeply about Disney and have contributed so much to this company," he said. "At the same time, these steps are notable if we want to be a company that moves faster, adapts to a rapidly changing environment, and keeps investing in the content and technology that will drive our growth.".

The cuts will help Disney fund its $26 billion in projected content spend for fiscal 2027, a 9% increase from fiscal 2026.

The entertainment giant is also forecasting double-digit growth in earnings per share in the next fiscal year, as well as segment operating income growth of around 8%.

Disney noted that the majority of that growth will be concentrated in the first half of the year due to the theatrical debut of "Avengers: Doomsday" and a boost from the Super Bowl, which will air on Disney's ESPN and ABC networks.

Industry observers note that "The growth is really going to come in the first half of this year," Johnston stated. "That's the opposite of what we saw in '26, where the growth was backloaded.".

Industry observers note that the tech giant will also increase its annual dividend to $2 a share, a 33% increase from the previously declared dividend. It will be payable in two installments of $1 per share, one in January and one in July.

According to recent reports, here's how Disney performed in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Oct. 3, compared with what Wall Street expected, according to LSEG:.

Disney reported net income for the fiscal fourth quarter of $2.61 billion, or $1.51 per share, compared with $1.31 billion, or 73 cents per share, during the same period the year prior.

Adjusting for one-time items, including severance and other restructuring charges as well as the value of intangible assets, Disney reported earnings per share of $1.77.

The tech giant's revenue for the quarter was 16% higher year over year, and results were once again lifted by its parks and streaming divisions.

Recent findings suggest that disney's experiences segment, which includes its theme parks and cruises, reported nearly $10.11 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year. Operating income for the unit increased 20% to $2.25 billion.

The division is already a top performer for the organization, but it benefited in the fiscal fourth quarter because of an extra calendar week compared with the previous fiscal year.

While international attendance continues to lag at Disney's domestic parks, it is being offset by domestic attendance, especially at the Walt Disney World resort in Orlando, Florida, Johnston noted.

Growth at Disneyland Paris was driven by recent investments including an expansion area called World of Frozen. Attendance at the Hong Kong and Shanghai parks remained soft because of broad economic challenges in those regions, according to Disney.

Still, D'Amaro stated he believes the growth in parks will be sustainable through next year, especially with new additions, including the "Monsters, Inc."-themed land "Monstropolis" opening at Walt Disney World in 2027.

Industry observers note that "Q1 forward resort bookings at Walt Disney World are pacing up compared to the prior year," he said. "And new capacity and new experiences will start coming online in 2027. We keep investing to make the experience fresh, and what we see is that drives repeat visits.".

Recent findings suggest that the tech giant expects operating income for the experiences segment to grow in the high-single digits in fiscal 2027. Growth is expected to be front-loaded as the company laps the launch of the Disney Adventure cruise ship, which set sail in March.

Over at its entertainment division, Disney saw revenue increase 17% to $11.89 billion. Operating income nearly doubled to $1.33 billion.

Revenue from streaming, specifically, rose 19% to $6.1 billion, Disney said.

According to recent reports, the segment benefited from the extra week on the fiscal calendar as well as from growth in subscription and affiliate fees. Additionally, the organization saw higher theatrical distribution revenue from titles like "Toy Story 5.".

Disney said Tuesday it expects operating income for the entertainment division to grow in the high-single digits in the coming fiscal year.

The company's sports division saw revenue increase 16% in the fiscal fourth quarter, reaching $4.61 billion. Operating income for the segment surged more than 50% to $1.39 billion.

Subscription and affiliate fees fueled this growth alongside an increase in advertising revenue.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer expects its sports division's operating income to grow by double digits in fiscal 2027. It noted that the fiscal first quarter of the year will see some declines because of the timing of College Football Playoff games and the New Year's window. However, the fiscal second quarter will benefit from the college championship as well as the broadcast of Super Bowl 61.

Disney's outlook for overall and segment results for fiscal 2027 excludes the impact of a 53rd week in fiscal 2026.

D'Amaro has made advancing technology a pillar of the company's growth strategy. In September, Disney hired Karandeep Anand in the newly created position of chief technology officer.

Industry observers note that "Technology is central to how we connect fans to more of Disney and drive returns on our investment," D'Amaro said on the earnings call. "[Anand has] been energized by how much opportunity he sees to move faster and go further in product and technology. Done right, that means serving our fans even better, working more efficiently and being more innovative across every one of our businesses.".

Disney announced a partnership with Adobe earlier this month to develop generative artificial intelligence models.

D'Amaro told investors that the team is exploring ways to use AI to make booking trips to Disney parks easier.

Sources indicate that "There's actually a vacation planning tool that's in beta right now at Walt Disney World. We built that with our partners at Google, and I've had a chance to experiment with it myself," he stated. "It'll be incredibly helpful for our guests who are booking trips. With these AI features, it can feel like you've got someone sitting right by your side, like a personal concierge, that intends and responds to the way that you want to actually book your trip to Walt Disney World.".

In a recent development, the entertainment company has also expanded its short-form content, adding a vertical video channel within the Disney+ mobile app. The company had previously announced a partnership with TikTok to bring creator content to the streaming app.

#93465. Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1112 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.
  • It has been revealed that the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD.
  • According to recent reports, now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.

It has been revealed that the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD. However, a large Latin cross carved into its lid dates to approximately the 10th or 11th century, suggesting that the person buried inside lived hundreds of years after the coffin was originally made.

According to recent reports, now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation. The remains likely belong to a prominent medieval monk, and researchers have narrowed the possible identities to two men who once led Westminster Abbey.

Two Medieval Abbots Emerge as Leading Candidates.

The fresh findings, published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the British Archaeological Association, come from Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

Rodwell identifies Aelfwig, an abbot who died around 1020, as the strongest candidate. At the time, Westminster Abbey was a Benedictine monastery, and Aelfwig had served there as a monk before becoming its abbot.

Industry observers note that another possibility is Wulnoth, who succeeded Aelfwig and died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey, making either a plausible match for the skeleton.

"We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," states Professor Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

"We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.

"The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.".

The elaborate burial provides another reason to suspect that the deceased held an important position. Rodwell suggests that the individual was 'honored' with a 'fine sarcophagus', an unusual distinction that would be consistent with the status of an abbot.

Rather than commissioning an entirely newly introduced stone coffin, those responsible for the burial apparently reused an existing Roman sarcophagus. The man's wooden coffin was placed inside it, and the stone lid was modified with a prominent Latin cross. This may represent an early example of recycling a valuable object for an entirely different purpose.

Upcoming Excavations Reveal the Skeleton's Age.

It has been revealed that the Roman sarcophagus and its mysterious occupant have fascinated researchers for generations. Rodwell's latest conclusions draw on several investigations conducted with specialists over the years, including work associated with Channel 4's Time Team.

In 2009, the television program examined the archaeology and architecture of King Henry III's original sacristy, located along the north side of Westminster Abbey.

Industry observers note that the same area was the scene of an earlier accidental discovery in 1820, when workers encountered the Roman coffin and broke its lid into six pieces. The damage was repaired around the time the sarcophagus was formally 'discovered' in 1869.

It has been revealed that more recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology, one of the UK's largest commercial archaeological and heritage organizations, carried out another excavation of the sacristy. Completed in 2025, the project was undertaken to support construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, a newly introduced facility at Westminster Abbey scheduled to open the following year.

As part of this investigation, human bone specialist James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA) conducted a fresh examination of the skeleton.

According to recent reports, his analysis indicated that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches tall. These findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the remains as those of a 'robust young man' no older than 30 and approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall.

Carbon Dating Confirms a 1,000-Year-Old Burial.

One of the most notable clues came from scientific dating of the remains. A bone sample was submitted to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon analysis, which produced a date range of 987 to 1052 AD.

Sources indicate that this places the burial firmly within the late Saxon period, centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was originally created. The dates also align with the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth, strengthening the case that the skeleton belonged to one of these medieval abbots.

"This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period.".

The results provide scientific support for the theory that an ancient Roman burial container was repurposed to honor an important religious figure nearly 1,000 years ago.

A Skeleton Thought Lost Was Hiding in Plain Sight.

The investigation also brought renewed attention to an unexpected discovery made in 2016. For years, researchers had believed that the skeleton was missing, leaving an notable part of the burial's history unresolved.

Sources indicate that that assumption proved mistaken when the sarcophagus was transported to a conservation studio. PCA researchers removed its lid and were surprised to find an almost complete human skeleton still inside.

The examination produced another clue that Rodwell describes as a 'remarkable fresh discovery'. Inside the stone coffin, researchers identified the rectangular outline of a structure that had disappeared long ago. Its shape was preserved by a white residue left behind by lime, a material historically used in burials.

Rodwell believes the outline marks the position of the original wooden coffin that held the deceased before it was placed inside the Roman sarcophagus.

"Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard," writes Professor Rodwell.

It has been revealed that together, the rediscovered skeleton, evidence of a wooden coffin, and newly introduced scientific dating have transformed researchers' understanding of this unusual burial. Although the man's identity has not been established beyond doubt, the findings suggest that a medieval abbot may have been laid to rest in a Roman coffin already centuries old.

Visitors can see the sarcophagus today in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

#93464. Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

Inside the Chinese City Where Furniture Dupes Are Made

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4652 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision.
  • Two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed.
  • Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision. The then 29-year-old doctor living in London finally pulled the trigger on plane tickets to visit Foshan, in southern China, for a flight later that same day.

Two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed. But Bekker was convinced that six days in Foshan to furnish her apartment—and possibly having all of the furniture shipped back to London—would still be cheaper than getting everything at home. With over 100,000 followers on social media, she also later turned her adventure into content, detailing her finds and their cost.

Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok. “When I saw that things like a sofa cost thousands of pounds, I was like, ‘OK, I’m convinced now that I’ll probably do something drastic to not have to pay that much,’” she claims. Her social media algorithm was already feeding her a radical solution. “Made in China, shit quality?” a Chinese furniture seller remarked in videos on Bekker’s TikTok feed. “Grass sofa? Our factory has mass-produced it; UFO table? Our factory has mass-produced it.” Soon, Bekker says, her “entire timeline became Foshan, Foshan, Foshan.” She learned all about China’s furniture capital, which each year exports nearly $10 billion worth of couches and beds and bathroom vanities, and everything else you could possibly need for your home.

Bekker is just one of a growing number of people around the world who order furniture directly from factories in Foshan. By either flying to the city—or through WhatsApp, TikTok, AliExpress, or Alibaba—buyers can commission made-to-order pieces. And most importantly, they can purchase dupes.

In 2025, Shirley Bekker flew to China to buy furniture, hoping that even with shipping the cost would be lower than shopping in London.

According to recent reports, duplicates were once primarily the domain of fashion and beauty, but consumers are now seeking out knockoffs of luxury designer furniture that promise the same quality as the original at a much lower cost—even after international shipping rates and tariffs. During the week of April 13, 2025, the number of videos urging Americans to buy directly from Chinese factories soared 250 percent. Tens of thousands of videos had been posted under hashtags like #ChineseFactory, and many of them were about furniture pieces. Some videos garnered millions of views and included contacts of Chinese sellers in the comments.

It has been revealed that @gabwithmeg, a working mom in California, claims on TikTok that she saved at least $100,000 by furnishing her entire house directly from China. “It is all Restoration Hardware and Arhaus-style furniture, and I’m going to tell you exactly how I did it,” she promised her followers in January. @gabwithmeg’s post received over 65,000 likes, and the comments are filled with owners clamoring to opt out of the traditional furniture market, if not bragging about having already done so.

Together, they represent a turning tide in furniture shopping for Westerners. If people can buy a couch that looks exactly like the famous Togo for $200 on AliExpress, why would they pay $4,800 for one from Design Within Reach? Sure, Ligne Roset is a legendary brand, famously crafting all its furniture near the French Alps, made by trained artisans using an almost entirely manual process. But not everyone cares about history, owning an original, or the ethics of intellectual property in design. In fact, some furniture buyers, including Bekker, aren’t even aware that some pieces they covet are copies. Bekker feels that designer furniture is more expensive because of the brand name, not necessarily the quality. “Sorry to say, for me, it’s a bit bullshit,” she indicates. “I’m really not one to buy into the idea that the name of the brand makes it worth the price.”.

According to recent reports, “We’re seeing the beginnings of a revolt against the brandification of everything,” says Christopher Sprigman, a law professor at New York University who has studied the knockoff economy. As a consumer, Sprigman expects brands to offer good and consistent quality, but there is a perception that “there’s no real quality control, there’s no real integrity, it’s basically just advertising and driving up costs, creating demand, creating desire without any real substantial benefit that the consumer can feel or taste or see,” Sprigman says.

According to recent reports, the videos Bekker saw never explicitly stated how much the furniture in Foshan would cost, but she was confident it would be far less than at the posh showrooms in London. Despite not speaking Chinese, she roamed around the furniture markets in Foshan’s warm and humid air. By the end of the trip, she had furnished her entire apartment for around £7,000 (about $9,200). Everything would go in a 20-foot container, embark from Guangzhou on a freight ship, and arrive at an English port more than two months later. Bekker’s videos attracted millions of views, and fans swarmed to the comments with the same refrain: “I have never been so influenced to go to China.”.

Four million people from over 150 countries visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture.

Everyone who goes to Foshan for furniture makes sure to go to the Louvre.

Sources indicate that in the central part of Foshan, the Louvre claims to be one of the largest furniture shopping malls in China, and likely the whole world. At over 4 million square feet, it’s bigger than its namesake in France, which is the largest museum in the world; 4 million people from over 150 countries and regions visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture. Past the facade—which looks like an outdated convention center with blue-tinted windows and rows of country flags above the entrance—is an opulent atrium with marble columns and gilded moldings.

It has been revealed that the complex was designed to be part of a tourist experience package, with official certification from the Chinese tourism bureau. There’s a shuttle bus from the nearest international airport and a five-star Sofitel hotel for guests. In addition to tourists from the US and Europe, there are ever more shoppers, architects, and traders from the Middle East, Africa, Russia, Central Asia, and South Asia.

According to recent reports, the Louvre contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones, so there’s something for everyone. As many of these brands construct their furniture in Foshan, it’s the ideal place for a showroom. Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics here, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “new Chinese,” and wabi-sabi. In most places, photography is strictly prohibited to “protect original designs.”.

It has been revealed that but the Louvre is often just a shopper’s first destination. “Foshan is not actually one furniture market. It’s a district, it’s a city, it’s an ecosystem,” indicates Claudia Hofmeister, an Australia-based furniture sourcing agent who has helped clients from around the world buy furniture from Foshan; she has personally traveled there at least six times. While the Louvre is the pinnacle of luxury furniture shopping, Foshan also offers other mid-tier wholesale businesses that are 100 percent Chinese, plus lower-end furniture brands that Hofmeister says she won’t touch. “And there’s a whole lot of other models like major supercenters just dedicated to lighting, tiles, and building supplies,” she says.

Industry observers note that for many travelers, the real shopping doesn’t happen there. The dupe factories, along with home construction and decor manufacturers, are a few miles away in Longjiang. Longjiang is known as the hub of furniture manufacturing, where you can find everything from fabrics to timber to metal parts. Its streets are lined with miles of furniture shops and nothing else. The town has its own exhibition center, but it stands in stark contrast to the opulent tourism spectacle at the Louvre.

The Louvre International Furniture Exhibition Center contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

According to recent reports, every March and August, Longjiang hosts its own furniture fair, which attracts small manufacturers, dealers, and domestic buyers from other parts of China. The furniture brands in the district care less about original design and are sometimes explicit about where they draw inspiration. On the facade of a showroom building next to the exhibition center, a billboard-sized banner advertises a “Lawrence sofa,” a popular 2017 design by the famous Italian brand Minotti that can sell for over $10,000. In their booths, some sellers display portraits of a white “art director,” an Italian flag, or plaster sculptures.

According to recent reports, even for Chinese people, the idea of traveling to Foshan to buy furniture instead of placing orders from home is relatively latest. As China’s real estate economy slowed over the past decade, the traditional business model of licensed furniture distribution struggled. Factories now have to contend with tariffs and competition from countries where labor can be cheaper. Sourcing companies position themselves to factories as a more direct connection to consumers. Even though buyers pay to travel, they can save “30 percent to 50 percent” while still gaining access to new designs and high-quality products, says Lin Fangfang, the founder and chairman of Yueanju, one of the earliest and most influential B2C furniture sourcing agents in China.

It has been revealed that yueanju, which was founded in 2016, says it has worked closely with the local government to develop the “travel to Foshan” marketing strategy. On the radio nationwide, ads hype shopping for furniture in Foshan, with organized pickups from train stations and airports, as well as customized factory tours based on specific needs and budget. A typical three-day trip costs as little as $170 per person. Agents take care of everything and even provide a cafeteria and nap area with recliners in Yueanju’s office building in Longjiang. “Even though [Longjiang is] only one bridge away, they just won’t come here because they don’t know about us,” Lin says. “[Now], we can accommodate over 200 visitors with no problem on this floor.”.

Services like what Yueanju offers rapidly exploded in popularity, bringing a steady flow of consumers to what had previously been a business-to-business manufacturing hub. They are now working with clients from countries including the US, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. In March, during Ramadan, the company hosted a group from Saudi Arabia. “They are royals, so their homes are pretty significant,” Lin says. The company customized the shopping experience based on their fasting needs, only going out after 3 pm every day to preserve energy.

Recent findings suggest that the modern history of furniture in Foshan started with a dupe. As the lore goes, in the 1970s a man named Li Jungang working at a carpentry factory got his hands on a couch from nearby Hong Kong, then a British colony. While upholstered furniture took off in Europe in the 17th century, traditional chairs in China were still made of hardwood and had no built-in cushioning. By the 1970s in Hong Kong, upholstered, Western-style couches were all the rage. Li cut open the couch, studied interior construction, and is said to have built what is considered the first-ever upholstered sofa in China. Similar stories citing the origin of Foshan’s relatively short history in modern furniture manufacturing are now proudly recorded in local history books, displayed in furniture showrooms, and retold by every entrepreneur in the city.

The Louvre in Foshan contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics at the Louvre, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “newly introduced Chinese,” and wabi-sabi.

The rest of the story tracks the rise of manufacturing in China. As the government started embracing the market economy in the late 1970s, China became the locus of offshore manufacturing for the rest of the world. Foshan’s voracious entrepreneurs and artisans saw an opportunity to remake the city—which until then was known more for kung fu and local cuisine—into a manufacturing powerhouse. The city became known for factories that specialized in building materials, home appliances, and furniture. Foshan’s home goods industry grew to include over 7,000 businesses that account for at least one-fifth of the furniture market in China. In 2025, Foshan exported $2.65 billion worth of furniture alone. “If you have a home, you have something made in Foshan,” indicates the promotional slogan and industry alliance launched by the local government in 2022.

It has been revealed that as the city became a furniture juggernaut, it developed an obsession with Italy and, more specifically, Milan, the capital of 20th-century interior design. At Salone del Mobile, the internationally renowned annual furniture fair showcasing some of the most innovative designs in the world, Foshan factory manufacturers study the latest luxury designs from Italian brands. A smaller number of companies bring their own products to the fair, and local furniture leaders also visit to help promote government collaborations between Foshan and Milan. In 2011, a Chinese newspaper reported that during that year’s furniture fair, Fendi Casa refused to admit Chinese visitors to its showroom. (Salone del Mobile did not respond to a request for comment.).

Industry observers note that some Foshan furniture makers do copy designs from Salone, and they do it fast. The 2026 fair ended on April 26; by May 11, Foshan furniture factories were posting on Chinese social media about mass-producing the Anywhere sofa by Edra, one of the breakout products of the year. “The first domestic upcoming Anywhere sofa is here,” claims a Chinese woman in a brightly lit showroom, walking past a sofa that looks identical to the original, on Chinese social media platform Rednote. The account, under the name HY Casa, says it’s a source factory in Foshan that specializes in “high-end Italian minimal made-to-order 1:1 furniture dupes.”.

To create a truly convincing replica, snapping a few photos in Milan is not enough. Wang Xunyong is the owner of EIBA, a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end dupes of Minotti sofas by ordering the original, shipping it back to Foshan, and taking it apart to study its internal structure, just like Li did in the ’70s.

A stack of pocket springs at the EIBA factory.

EIBA is a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end sofa dupes.

Before the success of EIBA, Wang had a series of failed ventures—restaurants and several other furnishing-related businesses. Eventually, he arrived at a decision: “Instead of doing a hundred mediocre things, it’s better to take one thing to the extreme,” he says in a video posted on his social media account. In 2023, he founded his current company with a small workshop model, leveraging his past experience in the furniture business. This time, it worked.

Wang’s factory in Longjiang occupies the fourth floor of a pristine white industrial building, where a polished lobby opens into a modest showroom/workshop. Several rows of finished sofas sit near the entrance beneath ceiling spotlights. Wang has a makeshift office area that he shares with his sales staff. Every so often, a Bluetooth speaker linked to his phone reveals in a flat robotic voice that someone has made a furniture order online. On the workshop floor, five or six women cut and sew sofa fabric, while several men shape foam, spray adhesive, and stretch upholstery over frames.

Wang has never been to Italy. His understanding of Italian design comes from sofas dismantled inside his factory. The first time Wang cut open an Italian-made sofa, he was struck by its complexity. It wasn’t just layers of materials stacked together, but rather a system with different densities, cutting methods, and structural logic working in harmony. He compares the sofa manufacturing process to making a cake: You can standardize the baking process by using a mold, but a complex curve would sometimes require human hands. For a long time, Wang notes, many factories focused only on replicating the look of luxury couches. The proportions and silhouettes of the sofas were similar to the originals, but the internal structure was oversimplified. But that misses the essence of what makes a piece of furniture great.

Lin Qi, a factory worker, cuts paper patterns.

Zeng Xiaofeng, a factory worker, cutting fabric.

Recent findings suggest that this path isn’t cheap. Purchasing original pieces requires significant investment, often eight to 10 times the price of the dupes his factory produces. Once the model is thoroughly studied, efficiency improves. Today, Wang says, his team can complete the reproduction of a fresh design within 45 days. This methodology has allowed his factory to reach annual sales of 20 million yuan (about $3 million). Unlike Minotti, which makes almost every piece of its custom furniture in Meda, Italy, Chinese factories can count on much lower costs for labor and manufacturing.

To outsiders, Wang’s work is ethically dubious, but he is unapologetic. “What we’re trying to do is copy it first and surpass it later,” he indicates. “Many people look down on copying others, but we ignore those noises. First, we learn their details and craftsmanship. Once you have the financial strength and vision, you’ll be much better equipped to do your own thing.”.

According to recent reports, in his view, as long as a product does not carry the original brand’s logo, it cannot be considered “counterfeit and substandard.” On a more practical level, he has developed strategies to reduce legal risk. Based on his understanding of regulations, Wang says, a piece is legally distinct if there are “seven points of difference,” even if that’s as minor as changing a board’s thickness from 3 centimeters to 2.9.

Wang’s rule of seven is a common belief among Chinese manufacturers, but it’s more folklore than law, states Morgan Pietz, managing partner at the Los Angeles office of Merchant & Gould, who has represented both sides of furniture IP lawsuits. “At least under US law, there’s no rule that if you make seven changes, you are good to go,” he says.

But it is difficult to legally claim that someone has knocked off a furniture design, lawyers say. In the US, most plaintiffs in the furniture industry need to go down one of two routes: Either they register patents for each of their products, or they need to demonstrate that a layperson would be able to discern the product’s origin. Both are difficult hurdles to clear. Design patents can cost around $5,000, including attorney costs and a filing fee for one product, and they only last 15 years; to make a “trade dress” claim, a furniture tech giant needs to show that its consumers recognize the design as being from a specific source. In most cases, furniture designs don’t rise to this level of scrutiny. And no matter which route one chooses, bringing the claim to court and enforcing it could cost millions of dollars.

Sometimes there can even be a correlation between the popularity of dupes and the sales of originals, Sprigman notes. When studying the luxury fashion knockoff industry in China, he found that buyers of counterfeit handbags can often move on to purchasing the genuine product once they become wealthier. “For some people, you could view dupes as a gateway drug to the traditional thing,” he says.

To Wang, the production of dupes is not only a furniture industry phenomenon but also indicative of how capitalism in China works more broadly. “Many of our industries started from scratch. If you want results as fast as possible, you have to learn from abroad first. Whether it’s equipment, aircraft, artillery, or high-speed rail, haven’t we always followed this same path?”.

International clients select materials at the EIBA furniture factory in Foshan, China.

Still, creating dupes is not a business that can scale infinitely. In Wang’s view, the market for copies has become oversaturated, and competitive price wars are eating into profit margins. Foshan brands are now pivoting to original designs, not only out of ethical concerns but also due to market pressure. One day, when he has enough financial capital and experience, he hopes to develop his own designs. And only then will he consider actually traveling to Italy. Not to copy their furniture, but to experience Italian culture and find inspiration.

“You need to truly immerse yourself in that environment to feel what high-end Italian design is really about” he states.

It has been revealed that almost everything in Nikki Brooks’ fresh house came from China, which is how she got the nickname “Container Girl.” Brooks, a TikTok influencer in Texas who finds “affordable fashion” for her followers, started looking for furniture for a new home in 2024. In the past two years, she has bought windows, doors, stone countertops, tiles, beds, sofas, and even a golf cart from Chinese manufacturers, enough to fill four shipping containers.

Sources indicate that in addition to her 150,000 followers across TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, Brooks organized a private Facebook group where over 25,000 members discuss how to source “high-quality, cost-effective materials from overseas—especially China.” In the group, people ask each other how to import, while others share photos of their containers arriving in the US or their beautiful homes stuffed with new purchases. Through affiliate marketing, Brooks also gets commissions from “some” products she recommends, according to her personal website.

“We’ve seen a whole crop of dupe influencers pop up, whose livelihoods are based on helping their audiences find the best deals,” states Sky Canaves, an ecommerce analyst at Emarketer, who spent over a decade reporting on China. According to Canaves, beauty and fashion influencers can take a 10 to 15 percent commission from the sales they encourage; in furniture, which is purchased less frequently, the rate can be around 5 percent, but the cost per item is higher.

While in Foshan, Bekker bought everything she needed for her upcoming apartment.

She decided to shop room by room.

In a recent development, A new generation of consumers—who came of age with Shein, Temu, and Amazon—consult TikTok or Pinterest instead of design magazines and often buy things directly through these apps. They rarely go to stores in person, if at all, and value affordability over virality. (See the Walmart Birkins, fake AirPods Max, Temu celebrity look-alikes, and everything else that’s been duped.).

“I don’t love the term ‘dupe.’ It sounds awfully cute for something that is essentially buying a knockoff, or a counterfeit, or a theft,” notes Coleman Gutshall, the vice president of strategic operations at Bernhardt Design, which develops high-end furniture with designers. From his perspective, an original piece of furniture is more expensive not because of an outrageous margin; Gutshall says his tech giant pays fair wages for over 1,500 employees in North Carolina and works with up-and-coming designers. Many iconic pieces that are duped today were conceived of by innovative designers 50 or 100 years ago, he says, “and in order to keep that continuing, you’ve got to have this constant pipeline of designers. If they can’t make a living through loyalty and through designing, then their talent is going to waste.”.

It has been revealed that but not everyone in the design industry is anti-dupe. “There is no way I could ever afford an original, newly introduced Togo sofa,” indicates Lauren Sinclair, an architect in New York. (A real three-seat Togo—the iconic foam-filled modular couch designed by French industrial designer Michel Ducaroy in 1973 and still handmade in France by artisans—sells for about $10,000 today.) In 2022, Sinclair paid a Chinese factory $200, plus another $700 for shipping, to get a sofa that looks just like a Togo but in a custom color and tailored to the exact size of her small New York City living room.

“As an architect, I typically frown on dupes. I know how hard designers work to get a finished product to market and how low the margins are for bespoke furniture design,” states Sinclair, who refrains from using them in her projects. In the case of her personal dupe purchase, she argues it’s ethically acceptable because the design isn’t fresh. “And even if I bought an official, original Togo sofa, would that money ever go to the designer, Michel Ducaroy?” she says. “Definitely not; he died in 2009.”.

Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too.

On the fourth day, Bekker spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair that she later learned was a copy of a piece designed by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer.

From her deep dives on TikTok, Bekker learned about furniture agents. But she knew better: Her mother, who has an international import business and regularly travels to China, told her to always avoid the middlemen. “She had already drilled it into my head from years ago that going with an agent means they’re asking the vendor to add a commission on top every time you are making a transaction,” Bekker says. Instead, her mom arranged for a Chinese friend to drive her around Foshan on the first day. Beyond that, she had to figure out everything by herself.

Recent findings suggest that bekker planned her schedule while on her China-bound flight. She decided to shop room by room. Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too. She posted TikTok videos capturing what she bought: a £350 sofa, a £150 coffee table, a £50 rug, and a £80 solid-wood dining table. Bekker wasn’t explicitly hunting for dupes, but they found a way to her. On the fourth day, she spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair, which she originally thought was over her budget. But the unusually high price prompted Bekker to look up the chair online through a reverse-image search. She discovered it looked exactly like a 2022 chair by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer, that sells for over £6,000 in the UK. That pushed her to purchase.

Shirley Bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip to Foshan has turned into a side hustle. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12.

​​In the end, Bekker bought everything she needed for her new apartment, even down to cutlery and bedding (customized with her own logo for an additional £10). She found a warehouse in nearby Guangzhou to store all her purchases before they were shipped to London. As soon as she got home, she started using her lunch breaks to compile a spreadsheet of price comparisons, which Bekker subsequently shared in detail on TikTok: how much each purchase cost her in China and, through reverse-image search, how much a similar item would have cost in the UK.

Industry observers note that bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip was starting to turn into a side hustle. Her followers kept asking how she found suppliers and how they could plan a trip to Foshan themselves. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12. Five hundred people have bought it since, she says. In September 2025, when Bekker posted a video about receiving the container in London, followers yet again rejoiced. “It’s been MONTHS! So glad this was brought back to me,” one comment reads. Bekker has since returned to Foshan three times, toured more factories, and opened a furniture sourcing agency to plan shopping trips for international clients. The last time she was in Foshan, she ran into a follower whom she had inspired to travel to China to shop for furniture.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Home Depot on Tuesday confirmed its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the tech giant, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.

Recent findings suggest that alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot stated Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.

Decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The company stated on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.

In a recent development, "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession blueprint.".

McPhail has been with the manufacturer since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.

"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.

In a recent development, he said the firm will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.

Home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the tech giant has previously said it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.

Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.

The CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The firm remarked comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.

Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Recent findings suggest that the company reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.

Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period.

"We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail said on the call with analysts.

In the third quarter, the manufacturer said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.

The company remarked it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.

For the full year, Home Depot said it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase.

Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

#93460. The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1680 w)

The $500 billion beauty industry's 'green' ambitions are a patchwork at best. And they're falling short

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.
  • 'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report highlights.
  • Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an key purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The escalating climate crisis is shifting many people’s purchasing patterns and this extends to the $500 billion dollar global beauty industry which is grappling with a range of sustainability challenges across product manufacturing, packaging and disposal.

'Delay means death': We're running out of ways to adapt to the climate crisis, fresh report highlights. Here are the key takeaways.

Strategy and consulting firm Simon Kucher’s Global Sustainability Study 2021 found 60% of consumers around the world rated sustainability as an key purchase criterion, and 35% were willing to pay more for sustainable products or services.

This shift in consumer preferences has propelled many beauty brands to set environmental goals: to move away from single-use and virgin plastics, provide recyclable, reusable and refillable packaging and offer more transparency around products’ ingredients so customers can ascertain how “green” their purchase is.

It has been revealed that however, consumers still struggle to understand the sustainability credentials of many products, according to the British Beauty Council. This is because the industry’s clean-up efforts have been inconsistent, and fall short of making a recognizable impact in the absence of collective goal-setting, global strategy and standardized regulations.

Industry observers note that there is no international standard for the beauty industry on how much product ingredient information to share with customers — or how to do so. Brands can set their own rules and goals, giving rise to confusion and “greenwashing,” where sustainability claims are often touted but not substantiated.

Companies often use marketing language like “clean beauty” to make it seem like their products are natural, for example, when they may not actually be organic, sustainable or ethically made.

After rebranding in the West, many beauty companies are still offering to 'whiten' skin elsewhere.

“The term ‘clean beauty’ has become quite dangerous. It’s used to sell more products,” according to British Beauty Council CEO Millie Kendall, who added that such buzzwords are losing traction in the UK as British customers wise up to their shortcomings. “Customers need better marketing information and certification information.”.

In a 2021 report calling on the industry to have “the courage to change” their business practices, the British Beauty Council wrote that, all too often, even natural ingredients involved in manufacturing products give way to “over-consumption, non-regenerative farming practices, pollution, waste and neglect.”.

“The only way out of this is transparency,” Kendall told CNN.

Jen Lee, chief impact officer at US-based brand Beautycounter, said she continues to see confusion over ingredients among consumers. (In 2013, the tech giant launched and published “The Never List,” which currently cites more than 2,800 chemicals — including heavy metals, parabens and formaldehyde — it claims to never use in its products.).

“Natural vs. synthetic ingredients has been a conversation. People think natural is safer, but it’s not always the case,” Lee explained. “Natural ingredients formulated in the industry can have toxic load. Heavy metals can occur in natural components of the earth.”.

Mother loses peripheral vision from apparent exposure to mercury in beauty creams. Toxic levels in her home put family at risk, say experts.

Recent findings suggest that “We used to be more natural and organic,” added Sasha Plavsic, founder of makeup brand ILIA Beauty. “What was challenging is (that) raw materials were difficult to source or would come in inconsistently or products wouldn’t perform.”.

Sources indicate that most makeup is created and molded at high temperatures, Plavsic explained. Purely organic materials often fall apart in this heat, leading to inconsistent results and subpar product performance. “Not every synthetic is bad,” Plavsic said. “Sometimes, it helps create the best in class formula.”.

The industry’s plastic packaging is a particular sustainability challenge — 95% is thrown away and the vast majority is not recycled, according to the British Beauty Council.

The cosmetics business is the fourth biggest plastic packaging user globally — after food and beverage, industrial packaging and pharmaceuticals — and plastic is about 67% of the industry’s packaging volume, according to Vantage Market Research. Beauty giant L’Oreal used 144,430 metric tons of plastic in its packaging material in 2021, for example, according to the Ellen Macarthur Foundation (EMF). Estee Lauder Companies reported its brands produced 71,600 metric tons of plastic in product packaging that same year.

And only 9% of the global plastic waste is recycled, according to a report from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. The United States only recycles 4% of its plastic waste.

Single-use plastic is wreaking havoc on the planet. Here's what you can do to minimize your impact.

Recent findings suggest that many brands are trying to phase out harmful plastics from their operations and adopt post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastic. (L’Oreal has set a target of 50% PCR plastic usage by 2025, while Estee Lauder is targeting 25% “or more” PCR plastic — but both are far from achieving their targets.).

Recent findings suggest that “Between 60-70 major global brands have made unprecedented progress” in PCR plastic usage across industries, EMF’s Plastic Initiative Lead Sander DeFruyt told CNN. But DeFruyt stressed that PCR plastic must be adopted in conjunction with brands removing single and virgin plastics from their usage cycles to truly make a difference.

However, PCR plastic is not easy to find — low recycling rates around the world mean there is limited supply. Meanwhile, demand for it is growing demand across industries, DeFruyt said. This competition hikes up its price, which is already higher than virgin plastic.

Hair care brand FEKKAI claims that it used up to 95% PCR content in its packaging, but pricing and supply issues posed a challenge, forcing it to presently aim for containers and packaging that feature at least 50% PCR in its packaging.

In a recent development, “PCR plastic is more expensive than stock plastic. The cost is hard and then sourcing it is too,” founder Frédéric Fekkai told CNN. “PCR is close to our heart, but there is a massive demand, so finding recycled plastic is difficult.”.

According to recent reports, beauty retailers plays a pivotal — and under-utilized — role, with control over stocking decisions and supply chains. But many vary when it comes to the standards they set for brands they sell.

Industry observers note that “Smaller businesses do more, full stop,” mentioned Jessi Baker, founder of the technology platform Provenance, which helps brands display their sustainability credentials for customers. “They move more nimbly. Some of them are born-good brands — climate friendliness was part of their setup. They don’t need to restructure their entire supply chain. Their culture already has it compared to the larger brands who need to work hard to change.”.

A history of beauty trends -- and the standards that shaped them.

Sources indicate that sephora launched its “Clean + Planet Positive” initiative in 2021, which labeled products that met its set criteria. (This is separate from the French retailer’s “Clean at Sephora” program, which is right now facing a consumer lawsuit alleging it carries a significant percentage of products understood by customers to be harmful.) Target launched a similar program in 2022, featuring a “Target Zero” icon for both online and in-store offerings that either have reusable, recyclable, compostable or reduced plastic packaging, or feature waterless or concentrated products.

Still, many steps taken by brands and retailers do not even begin to touch on the waste and pollution generated throughout supply chains, manufacturing and shipping, all huge problems for the industry to grapple with.

The gaps in standardization in the beauty ecosystem can, to some extent, be filled by certifications such as the US-born B Corporation, or B Corp. This accreditation, one of the most well-known in the beauty space, is issued by the non-profit B Lab, which scores a company on a variety of criteria around ethics and sustainability. However beneficial it may be among eco-conscious consumers, though, it is at the moment completely voluntary for brands to apply for.

Governments and multinationals enforcing regulations and setting a base line for brands to operate from when making sustainability claims would go a long way to making change, many experts and business leaders believe.

Susanne Kaufmann, founder of her namesake beauty brand, claims her efforts in Austria would reap better results if more countries around the world had stricter, more uniform garbage disposal laws.

A trash heap 62 meters high indicates the scale of India's climate challenge.

Sources indicate that “I package our product in a recyclable material,” Kaufmann stated. (Her products’ packaging, which is refillable and reusable, is made from 75% recycled plastic — and is 100% recyclable.) If I send this to the US, the garbage is not separated… and it’s not recyclable,” she explained, referring to inconsistencies in recycling laws across the United States.

Sources indicate that and when it comes to ingredients, the European Chemicals Agency lists 2,495 substances banned from use in cosmetic products marketed for sale or use in the bloc. But the US Food and Drug administration only lists 11, making it more challenging for American consumers to find safer, greener options. The Environmental Working Group, a non-profit watchdog, studied lab tests of 51 sunscreen products in 2021 and found that only 35% of products met the EU standard, compared with 94% that passed the US standard.

However, while government can set minimum requirements, Mia Davis, vice president of sustainability and impact at beauty retailer Credo Beauty, says the needle will move in the private sector.

Sustainable ships: The world's most eco-conscious cruises.

Industry observers note that “Regulation can raise the floor a bit. A person who doesn’t know about any (sustainability concerns) should still be able to walk into a bodega and get clean products… But that’s never going to be what the market can do,” she mentioned. “Market leadership is key.”.

In a recent development, in the absence of bold regulations or global standards on sustainability practices, this “leadership” — undertaken both by brands and customers in the beauty marketplace — is likely to be the most immediately impactful vector for addressing the industry’s climate shortcomings. It will take continued collective advocacy and initiative to see meaningful climate-conscious change.

#93459. Breaking: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

Breaking: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fresh observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole.
  • The center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment.
  • Over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fresh observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole. An international research team led by MPE has traced these compact clouds to a massive pair of stars whose powerful winds appear to produce material that could eventually help feed the black hole, known as Sagittarius A*.

The center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment. At its core sits Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), a supermassive black hole surrounded by stars, gas, and dust moving through a region dominated by intense gravitational forces. This extreme setting gives astronomers an opportunity to investigate how matter moves near black holes and where the material that sustains their activity comes from.

Over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*. These mysterious "clumps" may provide important clues about how material makes its way toward the black hole. However, scientists have struggled to determine where the clouds originate and what causes them to form.

Mysterious Gas Clouds Near the Milky Way's Black Hole.

One of the first major discoveries came in 2012, when astronomers identified a compact cloud of ionized gas called G2. Containing several times Earth's mass, the cloud produces emissions from hydrogen and helium, consistent with hot gas mixed with dust. It follows a highly elongated orbit around Sagittarius A* and has a faint extension trailing behind it, known as G2t.

Sources indicate that soon afterward, researchers examining older observations recognized another similar object, G1, traveling along a closely related path. The similarities suggested that G1, G2, and G2t might not be independent objects. Instead, they could represent concentrations of gas within a larger, continuous stream.

In a recent development, even relatively small differences in gas density can make such a stream appear broken into separate clouds. This happens because the brightness of the gas increases in proportion to the square of its density, making denser regions stand out much more strongly.

More recently, astronomers observed gas in G2's trailing material gathering into another compact cloud that follows a similar orbit. Although this newly formed object might naturally be called G3, that designation had already been assigned to a different object. Together, the related clouds trace a connected flow of material through the Galactic Center, known as the G1-2-3 streamer.

Industry observers note that these clouds could play a surprisingly important role in sustaining the black hole. Calculations suggest that if approximately one Earth mass of gas reaches Sagittarius A* every ten years, it could provide enough fuel to maintain the black hole's current level of activity. Discovering how the clouds form could therefore help explain how the black hole receives its supply of matter.

Astronomers Trace the Gas Clouds to Their Source.

Researchers have considered several possible explanations for the clouds, including powerful winds from massive stars, stellar explosions such as novae, and gas pulled away from objects by the black hole's gravity.

To investigate, the MPE-led team used two advanced infrared spectrographs, SINFONI and ERIS. Both instruments employ adaptive optics to produce sharper observations. By examining a specific hydrogen emission feature called the Brackett‑γ line, the astronomers measured the clouds' positions and velocities and reconstructed their paths around Sagittarius A*.

Recent findings suggest that the results revealed a striking pattern. G1, G2, and G2t all follow orbits with nearly the same shape and orientation. It would be extraordinarily unlikely for three unrelated clouds to share such closely matching orbital characteristics, strongly suggesting that they originated from the same source.

Two Massive Stars May Be Creating the Clouds.

By working backward from the clouds' observed motions and their velocities along our line of sight, the researchers identified a promising source: IRS 16SW, a massive contact binary system consisting of two stars in extremely close proximity.

Industry observers note that the stellar pair belongs to a disk of young stars that revolves clockwise around Sagittarius A*. Its location and motion provide a plausible explanation for the gas stream. Even the slight differences between the clouds' orbital paths can be accounted for by the movement of the two stars around one another.

Sources indicate that computer simulations of how gas flows and interacts provided additional support for this explanation. The models indicate that powerful stellar winds from the binary system can collide with surrounding material, creating a shock in the region between the stars. Gas then accumulates and becomes compressed, forming dense concentrations that can eventually separate from the system.

Once released, these compact clouds can travel inward along paths resembling those observed in the G1-2-3 streamer. This provides a physical explanation for how one binary star system could produce several distinct clouds moving along closely related orbits.

A Fresh Clue to How Supermassive Black Holes Are Fed.

The findings suggest that massive stars near the Galactic Center may provide a continuing supply of gas capable of fueling Sagittarius A*. Rather than relying only on material already circulating around the black hole, the system could receive fresh gas from the powerful winds generated by nearby stars.

It has been revealed that the discovery also brings together several important processes in astronomy. The evolution of massive stars, the movement and compression of gas, and the supply of material to supermassive black holes may all be closely connected. By identifying a possible source of the mysterious clouds near Sagittarius A*, researchers have uncovered a new way in which stars could help sustain black hole activity at the heart of our own galaxy.

Weapons, war and wavering trust: Germans want to see more restraint in foreign policy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home.
  • In a recent development, long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side.
  • In a recent development, in the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents noted they fear further military conflicts around the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for decades, German foreign policy was never seen as particularly controversial at home. The country was firmly integrated into NATO and supported EU expansion and cooperation across Europe. It also advocated for multilateral approaches to resolving conflicts around the world. All of this enjoyed broad public support. But all of this has also changed since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the wars in the Middle East. Now, Germany's foreign policy has become increasingly contentious and is fueling growing public anxiety.

In a recent development, long-held assumptions are beginning to crumble, including the belief that the US would ultimately remain firmly on Germany's side. This is one of the central findings of a new survey by the Hamburg-based Körber Foundation.

In a recent development, in the foundation's latest poll on public attitudes on German foreign policy, 65% of respondents noted they fear further military conflicts around the world. Meanwhile, 48% believe that Germany should adopt a more restrained approach to international affairs — a five percentage point increase from last year.

Since 2017, the non-profit Körber Foundation, established in the northern German city of Hamburg in 1959 by industrialist Kurt Körber, has conducted the annual surveys titled "the Berlin Pulse." For this year's study, the polling institute Forsa surveyed around 1,500 eligible voters in September.

The findings make one thing clear: The current government's approach under Chancellor Friedrich Merz — seeking to have a say in virtually every international conflict and drawing on Germany's position as the largest EU economy — is increasingly met with skepticism. Only 40% of respondents now favor greater international engagement, down from 48% in 2025.

Florian Bigge, who helped compile the study for the Körber Foundation, commented on the findings on Monday: "This is a significant decline, especially since we have been asking this question for years, with changes in the range of just two to three percentage points.".

Meanwhile, 77% of respondents want Germany to focus primarily on diplomacy rather than military action.

Sources indicate that the most dramatic shift in public opinion concerns the war in Ukraine. Germany's military support for the Eastern European country, including the delivery of billions of euros' worth of weapons, no longer has the backing of a majority of the population. In September 2026, only 46% of respondents supported continued military assistance, compared to 59% in the previous year's survey. Currently, a narrow majority of 53% want to halt weapons deliveries altogether.

As Jonathan Lehrer of "the Berlin Pulse" explains, opposition is particularly strong among supporters of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

In a recent development, "Eighty-eight precent of AfD supporters oppose military assistance to Ukraine," Lehrer noted. "This is an interesting finding, especially considering political developments in Germany, including state elections in which the AfD gained support by campaigning against aid to Ukraine.".

The AfD has recently overtaken the chancellor's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in nationwide polls.

Industry observers note that support for Ukraine was also the subject of a recent poll conducted by the opinion research institute Infratest Dimap. This study also found that public support for Ukraine is continuing to decline, with a majority now opposed to providing assistance (see graphic).

One finding from the Berlin Pulse study is particularly alarming for politicians and experts committed to transatlantic relations. As the US and China are increasingly seen as rivals on the global stage, 83% of respondents believe that Germany should remain neutral. Only 15% would side with the US.

In a recent development, this may stem from the policies of US President Donald Trump. Florian Bigge of the Körber Foundation said of the widespread preference for neutrality: "This sentiment is strong among Germans across all age groups and political parties. In eastern Germany, support for neutrality is at 92%, compared to 81% in the west. We interpret this as a desire for security but also reluctant commitment: Germans do not want to take sides in this conflict between the great powers.".

The picture becomes clearer when respondents are asked about Russia. Under President Vladimir Putin, 82% of those surveyed see Russia as a military threat. However, public opinion is more divided when Germany responds firmly to such threats, including hybrid attacks. For instance, after the attempted drone attack on Leipzig Airport in early May, Germany responded by closing the Russian consulate in Bonn. However, only 51% support such measures, while 46% favor a more restrained approach.

"The gap between external expectations and domestic support is the central challenge facing German foreign policy," mentioned Sarah Pagung of the Körber Foundation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

One matter that appears to cause relatively little concern among Germans is the conflict in the Middle East, despite the devastating situation in the Gaza Strip following Hamas's terrorist attack on Israel more than three years ago.

It has been revealed that this may also have to do with changing public attitudes toward Israel. One question in the study asked: "Does Germany have a special historical and moral responsibility for Israel's security because of the Holocaust?".

In a recent development, the results were striking: 61% of respondents said no, while just 36% answered yes. Among those under 25, opposition to Germany's special responsibility toward the Jewish state was even higher, at 75%.

This article was originally written in German.

💡 Key Takeaways
