  • In a recent development, he and partner Rylee Arnold have taken each challenge in stride.
  • “I have been really intentional about my life and making sure I don’t ever work really hard,” he notes, cheekily.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Comedian and podcaster Connor Wood has become a bit of a fan favorite on this season of Dancing With the Stars. “If we’re not in practice, I feel like I’m missing practice,” the 31-year-old tells The Hollywood Reporter on a Zoom call. It’s a rare rainy day in Los Angeles, and the season 35 contestant is finding a second to rest amidst crazy rehearsal schedules.

In a recent development, he and partner Rylee Arnold have taken each challenge in stride. The pair have found themselves amongst the five couples advancing to the show’s finale, airing Tuesday night. Wood’s viral social media moments have certainly helped endear viewers, however, his steadily improving dancing skills don’t hurt. Related Stories TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Season 35 Couples Perform Their Last Dances as a Winner Is Crowned in the Finale: See the Scores, Who Won (Updating Live) TV Where to Stream 'Dancing With the Stars' Season 35 Finale Live Online.

“I have been really intentional about my life and making sure I don’t ever work really hard,” he notes, cheekily. “This has changed that completely, flipped it on its head.”.

Heading into the final episode, he and the dancers are working with six hours a day of rehearsal to get themselves in prime condition. “Every minute of that is necessary for the show,” he notes.

Below, Wood speaks with THR about heading into the DWTS finale, the reaction to his viral Jennifer Lawrence moment and dealing with the online hate.

How do you feel going into the finals?

I feel really good. Me and Rylee, we went into the semifinals, and that was the hard part. It was two brand newly introduced dances, two long dances, two very fast hard dances, and this one is fun. We’re going out there, we’re putting on a show. It really is for us, which is fun. It’s for the fans, [but] it’s [also] for us. It’s something that hasn’t been seen before. We’re doing a really cool dichotomy of dances too.

What days are the longest for you?

In a recent development, the day after the show, we film basically what you see before we dance. We do all of the face-to-face interviews. We do the one-on-one interview, and then we do the group session interview. This is obviously a bigger one. There’s three dances, so they have three videos that they had to make. There’s one for each dance, and then they’ll film rehearsal and stuff for the filler. But I also have the podcast that I do, so that was 9 a.m. to 12 p.m., and then we filmed from 12 p.m to 10 p.m.

It was long, but it’s all needed. That’s the thing. Sometimes you go onto a set or something, and it’s like we’re doing a take for the 15th time, and I’m like, “I promise you I’m getting worse. Every time we do another one, I promise you’re getting a worse take from me.” This is not the case. This one you do get better as you put more hours in, which is an annoying, frustrating thing that that is true. The harder you work, the better you get.

What were you expecting for yourself coming in versus where you are now?

I wasn’t expecting anything for myself, honestly. I’ve only ever danced at weddings. I have no pride when it comes to sticking with something. I’m happy to throw in the towel. You’ll quit while you’re ahead. I’ll quit while I’m behind. I don’t think there’s any shame in that. I am competitive though, which is weird. We had to stop playing Monopoly in my family home because I took it too seriously. But that wasn’t part of this — I really can’t put my finger on why this clicked for me, but I leaned in a lot. I’ve done some really TikTok cringe things that I wouldn’t normally have done. It’s been so well received, it’s a vulnerability thing, I guess, that’s been nice to be a part of.

How do you get through these red carpets to make it an actually enjoyable experience?

According to recent reports, that’s my bread and butter. Hamming it up on the carpet with interviews, that is my Dancing With The Stars. A funny thing that I’ve realized is that obviously I’m not the best dancer on the show or even freaking close. I’m aware of that. I feel like people don’t realize that. I don’t think I’m Zeus on the dance floor. I’m very aware of what I’m capable of, but people also aren’t seeing that dance is a part of the whole of this show, and doing press and meeting fans and doing X, Y, Z, it all makes up that whole. Anytime we spend these 12, 15 hour days creating packages and personifying these people that are on TV, it helps the case. If they see that you’re working really hard, if they see that you’re having fun in the press lines. If you’re being vulnerable, and you’re oversharing, people really like that, they relate to it. That’s what that is. I look forward to doing interviews because that’s where I feel like I hit my stride on the dance floor is after the dance, and I can talk about how hard it was to learn in Argentine Tango.

Do you feel more confident in dancing now?

Yes, and I that’s a natural progression with this whole thing. I’m learning the dances faster because I’ve been learning dance for three months. There’s a baseline or a foundation that I’m pulling from. When Rylee gives me “Start here” and “do this,” I know what she’s talking about. I realized recently I’m personifying each dance. When a dance was really hard, I began to resent the dance on day two of rehearsal because I’m like, “We are not getting along, me and the samba, we’re not getting along. I don’t get the samba. It doesn’t make sense to me.” Getting past those couple weeks — I hit my stride in probably week six in this competition because I was not resenting the dance. It became easier for me to learn the dances. We saw my dancing. It’s not the best, but I am having a lot more fun because I’m enjoying the process way more.

With the show and being online, do you feel a bit of an overload? I’m sure you’re not looking forward to hearing “8th Avenue” or “smoothie” stated to you ever again. (Laughs).

I like when everybody’s on board with something. What a harmless thing for everyone to be having fun with. That’s good, clean, fun. It’s easy. I know a lot of marketing coordinators probably had a really great weekly meeting when they turned in their social media reports and they had a video with a million views on their page for brand X, Y, Z, football team X, Y, Z. Everyone had so much fun. Everyone got to put a spin on that. That fired me up.

In a recent development, the rest of the internet, totally different story right now. We’ve gotten to a point where I have become a bit of a villain for some people.

Why do you think they feel that way?

I think that they think that I personally voted their favorite off, and it’s like — I’m aware of my level of dance skill. I have nothing to do with me staying here. That’s just been just the dark side of making it as far as we made it. My understanding is that the more that people go home, the more the fans of those people will go to someone else’s page and villainize those people. That’s sad, and it’s just a testament to how invested people are in this show. A cool part of this show is that the fans are so invested. Like I said, the 8th Avenue thing, it’s fun for people to be a part of things. Being on the other side of that is not as fun. It’s part of the game. I signed up for it. I’ve never experienced that.

It has been revealed that it has to be tough given social media is a huge part of your job. You can’t disengage as much.

Yeah. As we’ve gone through the season… First of all, I’m like, “Well, not getting on Twitter the rest of the season. That’s a really interesting group of people.” You want to get home from the 15-hour day, and you want to lay on your couch, your Lola blanket swaddling you like a newborn. Turn off your brain, look at your phone. The first thing on your phone is, “Connor Wood’s still here? Who’s he paying at ABC?” OK, scroll to the next thing. But that is part of it. This is weird and sick in the head, [but] I am going to miss every part of this experience. If you have haters — you’ve been around long enough to have a hater — that means you’re doing something really, really well. I’ve been lucky enough. I will say, I’m not cut out for public scrutiny. This is not something for me. This will be my last reality show.

No Traitors in your future then?

According to recent reports, I mean, [if] they come knocking — Of course, I’ll open the door. But at least for Traitors, they’re going to take my phone. No, but it’s great. I’ve been lucky enough to make it this far, and it’s just part of the competition. We got a couple days left.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station.
  • The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft released atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov.
  • If all goes to blueprint, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station.

The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft released atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab.

If all goes to blueprint, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long.

Industry observers note that the cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module.

The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019.

Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com.

The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays.

Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere.

It has been revealed that japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only presently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

Industry observers note that michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #93455. Tech Report: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

Tech Report: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to upcoming findings shared with WIRED.
  • The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk.
  • Sources indicate that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to upcoming findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

Sources indicate that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” says Greg Pollock, the director of research at security organization UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”.

The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

Exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more crucial than ever to attackers.

The data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock says.

The China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He says the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

According to recent reports, pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, indicates that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.

According to recent reports, “Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he claims. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”.

It has been revealed that the larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler indicates.

It has been revealed that “After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how big it was.”.

According to recent reports, fowler claims there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.

Fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting tech giant, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.

Recent findings suggest that the enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.

#93454. Breaking: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1248 w)

Breaking: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1248 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reaching another star will require spacecraft capable of traveling far faster than anything humanity has built so far.
  • Some proposed interstellar missions would take this concept even further by using powerful lasers to push sails to extraordinary speeds, potentially reaching a substantial fraction of the speed of light.
  • According to recent reports, in a recent paper available on arXiv, Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology investigate how light interacts with a rapidly accelerating solar sail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reaching another star will require spacecraft capable of traveling far faster than anything humanity has built so far. Conventional rockets powered by chemical fuel simply cannot achieve the enormous speeds needed to cross the distances between stars within a practical amount of time. One promising alternative is the solar sail, a vast, lightweight reflective surface that uses the momentum of light to propel a spacecraft through space.

Some proposed interstellar missions would take this concept even further by using powerful lasers to push sails to extraordinary speeds, potentially reaching a substantial fraction of the speed of light. However, new research suggests that this approach comes with an unexpected complication. At extreme speeds, some of the very light driving the spacecraft forward could begin acting against it.

According to recent reports, in a recent paper available on arXiv, Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology investigate how light interacts with a rapidly accelerating solar sail. Their findings reveal a surprising source of resistance that emerges as the spacecraft approaches 75% of the speed of light.

How Light Can Push a Spacecraft Through Space.

Although light has no mass, it carries momentum and can transfer that momentum to objects it strikes. This creates a tiny pushing force known as radiation pressure. Under ordinary conditions, the effect is extremely weak, but in the vacuum of space, a large reflective sail can gradually build up speed as light continues to strike its surface.

Recent findings suggest that for spacecraft traveling between stars, powerful lasers could provide a much more concentrated source of light than the Sun. By directing an intense beam at a sail, engineers hope to accelerate extremely small probes to speeds that conventional propulsion systems cannot approach.

According to recent reports, the researchers examined three ways that photons, the individual packets of energy that make up light, transfer momentum to a sail. These interactions are incident light (that raw momentum of the photons hitting the sail), specular reflection (momentum imparted when photons bounce perfectly off the sail), and diffuse scattering (momentum from photons that are absorbed by the sail then reemitted in random directions).

According to recent reports, according to the study, these three contributions affect the sail's motion with different levels of efficiency. Incident light provides the strongest contribution in the researchers' breakdown, followed by specular reflection and then diffuse scattering.

A Strange Problem Emerges Near the Speed of Light.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated once a solar sail reaches relativistic speeds, meaning speeds high enough that the effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become notable.

Industry observers note that as the sail accelerates away from its laser source, it experiences an increasingly strong Doppler effect. This is the same basic phenomenon that changes the apparent pitch of a passing ambulance siren, except that light experiences a change in frequency rather than sound.

For the accelerating sail, the incoming laser light becomes progressively redshifted, meaning its frequency decreases from the sail's perspective. As a result, the light transfers momentum less effectively, reducing the thrust generated by all three contributions examined in the study.

In other words, the faster the spacecraft travels, the less effective its laser propulsion becomes. Even with a powerful beam continuously striking the sail, gaining additional speed becomes increasingly difficult.

It has been revealed that various concepts for interstellar exploration have been proposed over the years, including Breakthrough Starshot, which envisioned using powerful lasers to accelerate tiny spacecraft toward nearby stars. The upcoming findings highlight another challenge that such ambitious missions would need to consider.

At 75% of Light Speed, Light Starts Working Against the Sail.

The researchers identified an especially unusual effect once the sail reaches approximately 75% of the speed of light.

At this point, a phenomenon known as relativistic light aberration changes how the scattered light is distributed. Relativistic aberration describes how the apparent directions in which light travels are altered by motion at speeds approaching the speed of light.

From the viewpoint of an observer at rest on Earth, the diffusely scattered light becomes increasingly concentrated in the spacecraft's forward direction. Because emitting light carries momentum, the sail experiences a corresponding recoil in the opposite direction.

This means that diffuse scattering (admittedly the weakest of the three forces) begins producing drag rather than helping propel the spacecraft forward.

The result is a striking paradox: some of the light intended to accelerate an interstellar spacecraft actually begins resisting its motion.

Importantly, this does not mean the spacecraft suddenly stops accelerating or that its entire propulsion system begins pushing backward. The laser still generates a positive overall force, allowing the sail to continue gaining speed. However, the additional resistance reduces the efficiency of the system, making further acceleration more challenging.

Advanced Materials Could Help Overcome the Challenge.

The study focuses specifically on the forces produced by light and does not attempt to model every obstacle a spacecraft would encounter during an interstellar journey.

According to recent reports, for example, the researchers do not include resistance from interstellar gas and dust, which could become notable at extreme velocities. They also leave out the thermal challenges associated with directing extremely powerful lasers at a thin sail. If the material absorbs too much energy, intense heating could damage or even melt it.

Sources indicate that another important simplification is that the calculations treat the sail as an idealized mirror. Real spacecraft would need materials capable of reflecting laser light efficiently while remaining lightweight, durable, and stable under extreme conditions.

Sources indicate that engineers are already exploring advanced metamaterials and photonic crystals that could help address these demands. These specially engineered materials can be designed to interact with particular wavelengths of light in ways that ordinary reflective surfaces cannot.

In a recent development, intriguingly, such materials might even turn some of the relativistic effects identified in the research into an advantage. By carefully controlling how light scatters from the sail, future designs could potentially generate forces that automatically correct its orientation and position, helping it remain aligned with the laser beam throughout acceleration.

The Long Road to Interstellar Travel.

Despite the promise of laser propulsion, humanity remains far from building and testing a complete solar sail system capable of reaching another star.

In a recent development, the physics becomes increasingly complicated over such enormous distances and at such extraordinary speeds. Additional effects, including the curvature of spacetime, would also need to be considered in a more complete description of an interstellar journey. These effects were simplified out of the new analysis.

Nevertheless, understanding how light behaves when it interacts with a spacecraft traveling at a significant fraction of light speed is an crucial part of making interstellar exploration possible.

If humanity eventually sends robotic probes to another star, success will depend on solving countless engineering and physics challenges. Knowing that light itself can become an unexpected source of resistance gives researchers one more piece of the puzzle, and potentially a better understanding of how to design spacecraft capable of making the journey.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Six Indonesian projects, each from a director-producer pairing working on a debut or sophomore feature, have been chosen for the 2026 Indonesia-France Film Lab X MTN Lab, which runs Nov. 25-30 in Yogyakarta as part of JAFF Market.

Now in its third edition, the lab is run by the French Embassy and the Institut français d’Indonésie (IFI), with French film school La Fémis supplying the mentors. Indonesian partners include the Ministry of Culture’s Directorate of Film, Music and Arts, through its national talent management program, MTN, as well as the Indonesia Film Agency (BPI) and the Association of Indonesian Film Producers (Aprofi). The long-term aim is to seed French-Indonesian co-productions. Related Stories 'Grey's Anatomy' Texas Spinoff Casts 'How to Get Away With Murder' Alum Karla Souza in Lead Role ABC Schedule: 'High Potential' Season 3 Sets January Premiere, 'The Bachelor' Season 30 Rolls out in March and More.

“Indonesian filmmakers have never lacked stories. What they have lacked is structured access to international partners,” remarked Fauzan Zidni, chairman of BPI. “BPI is committed to working with the Ministry of Culture, the French Embassy, CNC and our industry associations to make sure these projects get made.”.

In a recent development, french script consultant Eric Collins leads the story development strand, working with each team individually to sharpen each project’s artistic vision and international prospects. A separate two-day industry workshop covers development, financing, international distribution and the workings of the French film business. It is led by producers Vincent Wang of House On Fire and Thibaut Amri of Avant La Nuit, along with Sébastien Chesneau of sales organization Cercamon.

The selection comprises “A Straight Way to Love,” written and directed by Kurnia Alexander and produced by Eliza Cheisa; “An Interesting Incident,” directed by Rizal Hanun, who co-wrote it with producer Janice Angelica; “Father Figure,” from writer-director Rizaldy Bagas and producer Mo Amputra; “My Tears, a Sea for Jakarta to Sink,” written and directed by Andrea Nirmala Widjajanto and produced by Nirartha Bas Diwangkara; “Saltstorm!,” from writer-director Al Ridwan and producer Utari Hanif Assyuri; and “Super Neli,” co-directed by Robby Ul Pratama, who also produces, and Anggi Frisca from a script by Resty Savira Oktaviani and Sally Anom Sari.

“It is particularly fascinating to discover how strongly traditional culture resonates in contemporary Indonesian storytelling,” mentioned Julie Tingaud, deputy head of international affairs at La Fémis.

Teams from last year’s edition get their next shot in December. The inaugural Southeast Asia Film Forum takes place in Paris Dec. 9-13, hosted by France’s CNC, the Centre Pompidou and the French cultural network. Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines are the four partner nations, and the program mixes panels, screenings and an institutional strand around a central slate of co-production meetings.

In a recent development, indonesia’s presence will be backed by the Ministry of Culture’s film directorate. BPI will take part in the institutional program, filmmaker Edwin will present two of his films, and the 2025 lab teams will pitch to French producers.

It has been revealed that fabien Penone, France’s ambassador to Indonesia, Timor-Leste and ASEAN, said the lab built on the joint cultural strategy adopted by French President Emmanuel Macron and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto at Borobudur on May 29, 2025, and that last year’s duos would arrive in Paris after a year of mentoring from La Fémis. “This is precisely our ambition: to turn the growing ties between our two film industries into concrete and long-term collaborations and, ultimately, more co-productions between France and Indonesia,” Penone said.

It has been revealed that the Borobudur declaration calls for a closer, more formal audiovisual alliance between the two countries, with co-production as its centerpiece. The Yogyakarta lab is one of the ways the two countries are building it.

The JAFF Market runs alongside the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival.

  • Nike noted Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.
  • Sources indicate that the retailer also laid out a financial framework and mentioned that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nike noted Tuesday ahead of its first investor day in nine years that it was reaffirming its 2027 financial guidance.

Sources indicate that the retailer also laid out a financial framework and mentioned that by the end of fiscal 2031 it's targeting approximately $5 billion in incremental revenue growth from fiscal year 2027, operating margins of 12% to 14% and adjusted earnings per share of $3.00 to $3.50. The organization said higher-quality revenue, gross margin expansion and productivity improvements would help it reach its goals.

Nike's 2027 financial guidance includes expectations for revenue to decline in the high-single-digit range, an adjusted operating margin of approximately 6%, and adjusted EPS of $1.15 to $1.35.

The firm also introduced a strategy it's calling Full Stride Ahead, which the company said aims "to get closer to athletes and focus resources on the greatest opportunities for long-term growth.".

Nike CEO Elliott Hill told CNBC's Sara Eisen that the newly introduced initiative is about "being closer to the athletes we serve.".

"What's different today is the depth and breadth we're taking from an innovation perspective," Hill said.

He added that Nike is emphasizing sportswear at a time when sports have never been more relevant around the world. Hill also remarked Nike is working to regain its cultural relevance, after a perceived dropoff contributed to its slowdown both in its home market and in China.

Nike remarked it would focus on performance sports and sportswear opportunities "with the greatest potential for long-term growth," and said its five priority sports would be running, training, global football, basketball and outdoor.

Nike is holding an investor day at its Oregon headquarters Tuesday as the manufacturer aims to prove to investors that its turnaround strategy is yielding success after a yearslong slump.

Sources indicate that last month, the tech giant reported mixed fiscal first-quarter results as it announced a restructuring plan, including layoffs that it noted would start next year. It's the company's third round of layoffs to be announced this year.

Nike's net income and revenue both fell during the most recent period compared with a year ago, and the organization said it expects revenue to decline by a high single-digit percentage in fiscal 2027.

The latest strategy, dubbed Pace, focuses on the company's supply chain and reorganizing into three geographies. Nike mentioned the turnaround plan is expected to deliver roughly $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031.

Nike has been seeing significant sustained declines in its China market, where revenue last quarter dropped 26%. Experts have mentioned the manufacturer is losing relevance in the country, while Nike has said it's actively working to win over younger consumers.

At the same time, Nike confirmed last quarter that it's creating a newly introduced global campus in India as part of its new growth strategy, hoping the country will help boost its performance. The company said it was remaining focused on China even as it begins to build out its India presence.

Nike COO Venkatesh Alagirisamy told CNBC the company sees an opportunity to triple its business in the country over the next five years.

He added that Nike's broader strategy will position it for success in India.

"If you look at the three components, brand building, landing those innovations into marketplaces in an increasingly locally connected fashion and then doing all of those things in a much faster pace really aligns well with the aspirations for India," he said.

CEO Elliott Hill's turnaround strategy includes improving different parts of the business at different rates based on priority. While it's seen some signs of progress in the North America business, Hill has said that performance isn't enough to offset the pressures on the firm elsewhere, including internationally.

The Nike consumer has also been under increased macroeconomic pressure as geopolitical tensions mount and inflation rises.

Shares of Nike have fallen 50% over the past two years.

Tech Report: Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence tech giant AdImpact released Tuesday.
  • Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.
  • The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence tech giant AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, stated that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions.".

Industry observers note that the record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

According to recent reports, the biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

In a recent development, it is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

Recent findings suggest that broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

Recent findings suggest that industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

The fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

#93447. Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (874 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (874 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut.
  • Sources indicate that the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract.
  • To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

Sources indicate that the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play vital roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the upcoming findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

To investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria.

The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

It has been revealed that these medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as notable as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," said Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

This discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone presently takes may overlook an crucial part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics.

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

It has been revealed that researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

The researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped.

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

By examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

It has been revealed that although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

In a recent development, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought.

The findings point to an important consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

Sources indicate that the results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

"This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," said Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jenna Ushkowitz, who starred as Tina Cohen-Chang for the entirety of “Glee,” is reflecting on how the Fox series addressed the real-life death of her fellow cast member Cory Monteith, and why she now feels it “wasn’t the right thing” to do at the time.

Industry observers note that monteith played Finn Hudson, the show’s leading man and quarterback-turned-Glee club member, until he died of an accidental overdose in July 2013. The show honored the actor with a Season 5 episode titled “The Quarterback” that October, a tribute to Monteith that also explained Hudson’s passing within the context of the show. (The episode makes no mention of how Hudson died.) Related Stories 'Grey's Anatomy' Texas Spinoff Casts 'How to Get Away With Murder' Alum Karla Souza in Lead Role ABC Schedule: 'High Potential' Season 3 Sets January Premiere, 'The Bachelor' Season 30 Debuts in March and More.

Recent findings suggest that “To shoot [the tribute episode] ‘The Quarterback’… I think it wasn’t the right thing,” Ushkowitz noted on the “We Need to Talk” podcast Monday. “And I think everybody collectively agrees that it’s maybe not the thing that we should have done, because we were grieving both privately and publicly.”.

According to recent reports, “I think the fans definitely needed something, because they loved Cory so dearly like we did, and [loved] Finn so dearly,” she said. “But it’s a really hard thing to be grieving your friend and be a character grieving their friend at the same time.”.

“It was like, too soon for that. [It] was not fun, [I] don’t want to remember that time,” she continued. “The show itself was never the same. He was the heart of the show, our friend, most importantly, and our leader. He really was the quarterback for us. He held everybody together. He hosted parties for the crew. He was the kindest. He knew everybody’s names. He just was such a good person, a kind person.”.

Ushkowitz also noted that the “nobody” on the show “had the tools to deal with” Monteith’s death. “Even our creators, they were dealing with grief too. So nobody had the tools.”.

“Glee” first premiered in Sept. 2009, and in addition to Monteith and Ushkowitz, starred Lea Michele, Naya Rivera, Dianna Agron, Matthew Morrison, Jane Lynch, Heather Morris, Chris Colfer and more. A reboot of the show was set at Disney+ and Hulu in October.

It has been revealed that speaking with Variety earlier this month, co-creator Ian Brennan said he’s “really excited about it.” “It’s going to be a lot of fun,” he added. “We’re still figuring a lot of it out,” Brennan said on addressing the deaths of Monteith and Rivera, who died in 2020. “That’s going to be part of it, that sadness and that loss. But still in all, I think [“Glee”] is too big of a thing to sort of let lay. There’s something about that feels right right now.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that china has launed an international astronaut to its Tiangong space station today (Nov.
  • A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m.
  • You can watch the liftoff live here at Space.com, courtesy of China Central Television (CCTV).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that china has launed an international astronaut to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program.

A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25).

You can watch the liftoff live here at Space.com, courtesy of China Central Television (CCTV).

Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong, a three-module station that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022.

Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever debuted a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023.).

According to recent reports, china and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025, with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training.

Sources indicate that we didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China unveiled the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch.

This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest.

It has been revealed that ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which debuted in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu.

Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24.

According to recent reports, according to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

#93442. What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (677 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

What happens if a nuclear weapon explodes in space?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (677 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth.
  • According to recent reports, in the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas.
  • We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A nuclear explosion in space would be unlikely to cause widespread injuries on Earth. But it could disable satellites that provide services we depend on every day, including some that save lives.

According to recent reports, in the United States, satellite failures could make it harder for emergency crews to communicate in remote areas. If GPS were also disrupted, drivers and pilots could lose navigation guidance, and financial networks could lose a source of precise time.

We have some idea of what would happen because it's already been done.

In a recent development, on the evening of July 8, 1962, people in Hawaii held "watch-the-bomb parties" and followed the countdown on shortwave radio. Then the night sky lit up. The United States had detonated a nuclear weapon about 400 kilometers (250 miles) above the Pacific. The test was called Starfish Prime.

It has been revealed that an electromagnetic pulse knocked out some streetlights in Hawaii, and some Pacific radio links briefly went down. The glow faded within minutes, but some satellites failed months later.

Recent findings suggest that the air was too thin for a conventional fireball to form or for a destructive shock wave to reach the ground. Charged particles made denser air below glow, creating an artificial aurora. The atmosphere also absorbed much of the initial radiation.

Satellites are especially vulnerable because they orbit above most of the atmosphere that shields people on the ground from the initial radiation.

In orbit, the initial burst of X-rays can damage spacecraft right away. But Earth's magnetic field can also trap electrons released after the blast, as it did after Starfish Prime. Satellites receive another dose each time they cross the resulting radiation belt. Over time, that exposure can damage electronics and solar panels.

That would depend on where the explosion happened and which satellites crossed the radiation belt. GPS satellites send signals that help phones, planes and ships work out where they are. They orbit about 20,200 kilometers above Earth and could keep working even if satellites closer to Earth failed.

Industry observers note that but satellites do different jobs. A ship's emergency beacon can use GPS to work out its location, then send it to rescuers through a separate satellite network. If part of that network failed, the alert could take longer to get through.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars its parties from placing nuclear weapons in orbit. The 1963 Limited Test Ban Treaty prohibits its parties from carrying out nuclear explosions in space.

Industry observers note that the Outer Space Treaty has no dedicated system for checking what spacecraft carry. A detonation is easier to detect because US satellite sensors are designed to pick up the signals it gives off.

Recent findings suggest that shielding could help protect satellite electronics, and backups could keep some services running. During a GPS outage, pilots over the contiguous US can use ground-based navigation aids. Operators could launch replacements, but those satellites could still face lingering radiation or debris.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Radiation could leave many satellites intact but unable to steer. If two objects collided, fragments from the crash could hit other satellites, creating more debris and triggering further collisions. If enough debris built up for the chain reaction to keep going on its own, it could continue even if no newly introduced satellites were launched. This is known as Kessler syndrome.

Industry observers note that whether an explosion would trigger such a cascade is uncertain. If it did, the debris could endanger replacement satellites for years.

In a recent development, some radioactive particles could enter the atmosphere and eventually settle on the ground. But a blast in space is too far away to sweep up the soil and water that carry fallout from a surface explosion.

As the particles disperse, their radioactivity decreases over time. The concentrated local fallout that can expose people near a ground-level blast to high doses would be unlikely.

#93441. After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1626 w)

After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object.
  • Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission.
  • It has been revealed that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that after eight years in space and a journey covering 10 billion kilometers, a pioneering X-ray telescope traveling to Mercury has captured its first observations of a distant cosmic object. The instrument, built in the UK, successfully detected X-rays from the Crab Nebula, one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky, marking an key milestone for the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's BepiColombo mission.

Scientists at the University of Leicester are now evaluating the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), which is traveling aboard the two-spacecraft mission. Their initial results are highly encouraging, arriving just as BepiColombo prepares to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21.

It has been revealed that the telescope has spent eight years traveling through space, making it essential to confirm that its delicate components are still working properly. Although engineers monitored MIXS throughout the journey, the instrument could not look directly into space until September. That opportunity came after the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the two science orbiters, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) or Mio.

With its view finally unobstructed, MIXS could begin the critical tests needed before the spacecraft enters its planned orbit around the solar system's smallest planet.

A Telescope's First Look Across 6,500 Light-Years.

Sources indicate that for its first astronomical target, the team selected the Crab Nebula, located approximately 6,500 light-years from Earth. This well-studied remnant of an exploded star produces a strong, predictable X-ray signal, making it an ideal reference for testing the telescope's performance.

By examining how MIXS observes this distant object, researchers can determine whether the instrument still performs as expected after its lengthy journey. They can also compare the results with laboratory measurements collected in 2015, when the telescope was last tested on Earth.

The main observation campaign took place on September 11 and 12. Over 39 hours, the spacecraft carried out 55 carefully controlled changes in orientation to collect the data.

Sources indicate that one important measurement was the telescope's angular resolution, which describes its ability to distinguish small details in an image. Scientists determined this by examining how widely the Crab Nebula's X-ray signal spread across the detector. Remarkably, MIXS delivered slightly sharper resolution than it had during its laboratory tests in 2015.

That improvement is particularly encouraging because the instrument will eventually use its X-ray vision to investigate the composition of Mercury's surface.

Better Than Expected After Eight Years in Space.

Professor Emma Bunce, Principal Investigator (PI) for MIXS and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester, welcomed the results as a major achievement for the international team responsible for developing the instrument.

Sources indicate that professor Bunce remarked: "We have waited a long time to make measurements with MIXS and it is fantastic to see it operating brilliantly in space. This is testament to our engineering and technical team, and our international partners who we have worked with over many years to build this incredible instrument. 80% of the technology on MIXS is newly introduced!

Industry observers note that "During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out. We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the Sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after 8 years in space.

"We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase.".

It has been revealed that the results suggest that the telescope has weathered its long exposure to the harsh space environment exceptionally well. Engineers have found no unwanted visible light interfering with its images, and the effects of high-energy cosmic rays are understood well enough to be removed during data processing.

Sources indicate that the team has also identified a small amount of X-ray emission originating within the instrument itself when sunlight strikes its optics. However, this effect is not expected to interfere with observations of Mercury's sunlit surface. Most importantly, the detector reveals no signs of radiation damage after eight years in space.

Some remaining effects still require investigation, and scientists expect to make further adjustments after the spacecraft reaches Mercury to ensure that MIXS is ready for its full scientific mission.

How X-Rays Will Reveal Mercury's Hidden Chemistry.

In a recent development, bepiColombo is designed to investigate Mercury in unprecedented detail. As the smallest and one of the least explored rocky planets in our solar system, Mercury offers scientists a rare opportunity to understand how planets form and change under the extreme conditions found close to a star.

One of the mission's major goals is to uncover the planet's chemical composition and geological history. These findings could help explain Mercury's unusual characteristics while providing broader insights into the formation and evolution of the solar system.

MIXS, carried aboard the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), will play a central role in this investigation. Developed by a European consortium led by the University of Leicester, it draws on the university's long history of X-ray astronomy research.

It is the first imaging X-ray telescope to operate on a planetary science mission. Working alongside other scientific instruments, MIXS will help produce a global map showing the elements that make up Mercury's surface, revealing its atomic composition in greater detail than ever before. It is also the only UK-led scientific instrument aboard BepiColombo and receives support from the UK Space Agency.

According to recent reports, the instrument works by detecting fluorescent X-rays released by rocks on Mercury's surface. When powerful X-rays from the Sun strike these rocks, they can cause atoms within the material to emit X-rays of their own. Different elements produce characteristic X-ray signals, allowing scientists to identify what the surface is made of without collecting physical samples.

MIXS will make these measurements with assistance from the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), which monitors the solar radiation and particles reaching Mercury.

Sources indicate that the telescope will also examine X-rays emitted from Mercury's nighttime surface when charged particles associated with the planet's magnetic environment strike it. These measurements could reveal key connections between Mercury's surface and the surrounding space environment.

A 10 Billion Kilometer Journey With a Personal Legacy.

Recent findings suggest that for Dr. Adrian Martindale, MIXS Instrument Scientist at the University of Leicester's School of Physics and Astronomy, the successful observations represent the culmination of more than two decades of work.

Martindale joined the project in 2003 while still an undergraduate student and has been involved in nearly every aspect of the instrument's development.

Sources indicate that dr. Martindale said: "BepiColombo, and MIXS in particular, are like part of my family. I've been involved since I was an undergraduate and touched almost every part of the instrument before it was debuted.

"This first data is mind-blowing to me. The last time we could see through this telescope it was in the basement under the School of Physics and Astronomy in Leicester, but after a rocket launch, eight years in space and 10 billion kilometers traveled it looks just the same. I can't wait to see the science data it produces when we get into orbit.".

It has been revealed that the milestone also carries special meaning for the team because MIXS represents the scientific legacy of Professor George Fraser. Fraser was the instrument's original Principal Investigator and the driving force behind its innovative optical design before his death in March 2014.

Professor Bunce added: "We are thinking of George as we operate MIXS fully in space for the first time and know that he would be very, very proud of the team and delighted at our first light observations.".

BepiColombo Prepares for Its Final Arrival at Mercury.

BepiColombo began its arrival phase on September 3, when the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) separated from the spacecraft assembly.

The remaining connected spacecraft are scheduled to enter orbit around Mercury on November 21. The two science orbiters, MPO and Mio, are then expected to separate on December 9 to 10, allowing them to prepare for their respective scientific operations.

The mission's primary science phase is scheduled to begin in April 2027. Once underway, BepiColombo will investigate Mercury's surface, internal structure, magnetic field, and surrounding environment, helping scientists piece together the history of a planet that remains surprisingly mysterious despite its proximity to the Sun.

For the MIXS team, the successful first observations of the Crab Nebula offer an early indication of what the instrument may accomplish when it finally turns its attention to Mercury.

International Collaboration and Funding.

Industry observers note that MIXS was developed through a partnership involving research institutions and technology companies across Europe. Participating organizations include:.

UK funding for the BepiColombo MIXS instrument comes from the UK Space Agency, which serves as the lead funding organization, along with STFC, the European Space Agency, and the University of Leicester.

The renewal was confirmed during the season 35 finale of DWTS on Tuesday night, which saw Tatyana Ali, Ezra Frech, Amber Glenn, Maura Higgins and Connor Wood compete for a chance to win the season 35 Len Goodman mirrorball trophy.

It has been revealed that zaikman reflected on winning The Next Pro in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter, saying taking on the show had been “a dream come true.” She added, “I’ve been a competitive dancer for all my life, and we have certain rules that we have to follow. The Next Pro allowed me to figure out who I am on a deeper level as a dancer. What can I bring to the dance floor? Maybe something fresh that people haven’t seen before. [On DWTS,] you can break the rules. You can be more creative.”.

Recent findings suggest that THR also recently asked Next Pro judge and season 35 pro dancer Mark Ballas if he’d be open to returning to the judges panel for a potential second season. “I don’t know if they’re doing a second season yet. I’ve had no confirmation of that. But yeah, again, if the timing feels right and everything’s in line with my family, and it makes sense, then sure. It was a fun experience,” he said.

Dancing With the Stars: The Next Pro is produced by BBC Studios. Conrad Green serves as showrunner and executive producer. Deena Katz, Ryan O’Dowd, Krystal Whitney and Alex Cross are executive producers. Quinn Lipton is co-executive producer.

Breaking: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1043 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.
  • In a recent development, the Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence.
  • In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking upcoming ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

In a recent development, the Pan American Health Organization announced the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking upcoming ones.

Industry observers note that "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

It has been revealed that more than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in Fresh York and two in Wisconsin.

The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas said during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

According to recent reports, the U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action initiative in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention mentioned it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

According to recent reports, CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz mentioned in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

In a recent development, last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

It has been revealed that the decision also poses a upcoming test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, mentioned he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles.".

Recent findings suggest that "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy stated. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.".

CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

In a recent development, the MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

Sources indicate that "We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood said in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.".

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," stated Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

According to recent reports, based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

Industry observers note that the U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.
