German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

📅 24 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life.
  • Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
  • "Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.

Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.

"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

According to recent reports, when the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale promptly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.

US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a latest title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.

Shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

In a recent development, "We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it.".

The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.

"We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person.".

While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.

The pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a New York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he revealed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Recent findings suggest that felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.

Industry observers note that later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.

"The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown upcoming ways to resolve conflicts.".

According to recent reports, "And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a substantial studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story.".

And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.

They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they stated, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge.".

The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.

Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

It has been revealed that for their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer remarked: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

Recent findings suggest that for the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.

And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.

Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.

The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they stated; then no one would have seen it.

They have a clear message for young creatives.

It has been revealed that "Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors.".

It has been revealed that what started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.

This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • According to recent reports, the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m.
  • The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.

According to recent reports, the historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.

The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.

Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth.

Astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.

According to recent reports, light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.

Even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

It has been revealed that voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.

The milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.

A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were introduced in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.

Industry observers note that managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary upcoming details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.

Industry observers note that today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.

"Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.".

Recent findings suggest that "Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," stated Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward upcoming frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.".

Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth.

The Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.

The records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that launched them.

Sources indicate that "Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," stated Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.".

Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun.

Voyager 1 is currently moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

Industry observers note that this protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.

In a recent development, voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.

One of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising fresh questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.

"The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.".

How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years.

Industry observers note that operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.

Electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.

Voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.

Recent findings suggest that as the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.

The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.

One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars.

In a recent development, maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.

It has been revealed that despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.

Recent findings suggest that "We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," stated Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars.".

‘Dancing With the Stars’: All 35 Winners

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hollywoodreporter

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s been two decades since Dancing With the Stars crowned its first winner.
  • Recent findings suggest that far before TikTok caught on to the merit the reality television series offers, ABC has been crowning winners of the show year after year.
  • To celebrate the success of the series and commemorate its various champions who were crowned before the series earned its newfound virality, The Hollywood Reporter has rounded up all 35 winners of Dancing With the Stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s been two decades since Dancing With the Stars crowned its first winner. What started as a family-friendly dance competition show for a unique pool of celebrities has transformed into a cultural phenomenon.

Recent findings suggest that far before TikTok caught on to the merit the reality television series offers, ABC has been crowning winners of the show year after year. Dancing With the Stars has attracted quite an impressive slate of stars throughout its tenure, and a select few of them (35, to be exact) have snatched that mirrorball trophy and earned the coveted title of “winner.”.

To celebrate the success of the series and commemorate its various champions who were crowned before the series earned its newfound virality, The Hollywood Reporter has rounded up all 35 winners of Dancing With the Stars.

This story was originally published in November 2025, and is updated as fresh winners are confirmed.

It has been revealed that kelly Monaco won the inaugural season of DWTS in 2005 alongside pro dancer Alec Mazo. That was far from the last time the General Hospital actress would be seen in the ballroom, as she notably competed on the 15th season with Valentin Chmerkovskiy as her partner.

Her double spin as a contestant on the series makes her one of six winners to return to the show to compete for a second time. She also appeared on season 25 to perform a trio number with Terrell Owens and Cheryl Burke, alongside six other former competitors.

It has been revealed that drew Lachey, former member of 98 Degrees and brother to Love Is Blind host Nick Lachey, picked up his mirrorball during season two. Partnered with Cheryl Burke, he returned for season 15 where he competed with Anna Trebunskaya.

Despite being named the show’s champion on his first DWTS turn, he was eliminated during week three during his second shot. However, Lachey, alongside Monaco, is still penned in the DWTS history books as one of the few winners to compete on the show more than once.

It has been revealed that cheryl Burke extended her winning streak into season three with Emmitt Smith. The former Dallas Cowboys running back made history with his 2006 win as the first (of four) NFL players to win DWTS. Plus, Smith is a part of the hexad of past champions who returned for season 15, where he was partnered with Cheryl once more.

Olympian Apolo Anton Ohno won the fourth DWTS installment, notably earning current co-host Julianne Hough her first mirrorball. Plus, Julianne’s season four victory also set the record for the youngest pro dancer to reign supreme, as she won the competition series at just 18 years old. (And she quickly made another record one year later.) Ohno also returned for season 15, and placed fifth.

Industry observers note that julianne Hough followed in Cheryl Burke’s footsteps in 2007 by winning the show for the second year in a row with racing driver Hélio Castroneves. The Indy 500 racer came back to DWTS in 2015 for season 15, where he placed 10th.

Olympic champion figure skater Kristi Yamaguchi translated her gold-medal winning talents into the DWTS ballroom in 2008, where she won season six. Her triumph saw Mark Ballas earn his first win as a pro dancer, one of many more to come.

It has been revealed that brooke Burke and current judge Derek Hough won the show’s seventh installment, which led to years of them both being intertwined with the DWTS family. Coming onto the show as a model and TV host, Burke offered the latter talent to the series as a DWTS co-host from season 10-17.

Brooke’s win was also served as Derek’s first win. While this list is intended to highlight the winners of the show, it’s also important to note that each celebrity victory also parlayed into the careers of the pro dancers that make up the series.

Shawn Johnson became the first gymnast to win DWTS in 2009. Partnered with Mark Ballas (marking his second victory), the gold medalist reappeared on the series for (you guessed it!) season 15 alongside Derek Hough.

According to recent reports, donny & Marie star Donny Osmond took his turn on the competition ballroom dance series in 2009, where he won season nine alongside Kym Johnson. He is notably the oldest person to ever win the show, as he was 51 at the time he was crowned champion.

Before Nicole Scherzinger won her Tony Award, she reigned victorious on DWTS. The former Pussycat Dolls singer was partnered with Derek Hough for the landmark 10th season.

Recent findings suggest that derek Hough won his fourth DWTS installment during season 11, with Dirty Dancing actress Jennifer Grey. Her first dance paid tribute to the film, a Viennese waltz set to “These Arms of Mine” by Otis Redding from the movie.

Grey long held the record for the most perfect scores in a season, setting it initially with six. She stands as the eldest woman to win DWTS, and she was 50 when she secured the title.

Former Pittsburgh Steelers player Hines Ward nabbed the DWTS season 12 champion title in 2012 with Kym Johnson.

Recent findings suggest that actor and Army veteran J.R. Martinez won season 13 alongside pro Karina Smirnoff, marking her first DWTS win. Following his victory, Martinez told The Hollywood Reporter he was “so grateful that I was able to be part of the journey to help get her first mirrorball trophy.”.

Donald Driver, a former Green Bay Packers player, and Peta Murgatroyd won season 14 of DWTS. Following the triumph, he reflected on becoming another NFL star to win the mirrorball with THR.

It has been revealed that “It took me 13 years to win the Super Bowl,” Driver joked. “I’m just glad it took me one season to win the mirrorball.”.

The coveted 15th season of the show, better known as DWTS: All-Stars, was ultimately won by Melissa Rycroft. She was a contestant on The Bachelor season 13, and got engaged to Jason Mesnick, though he called off the engagement shortly after.

Sources indicate that after her run as a Bachelor Nation star, she promptly pivoted to appearing on DWTS for season eight. (It’s a trend that would later catch wind for contestants in the franchise to go on the competitive dance show directly after their time searching for love on TV.) There, she placed third, before returning for season 15 and winning the mirrorball alongside Tony Dovolani.

It has been revealed that american Idol alum Kellie Pickler returned to the competitive reality TV circuit in 2013, earning first place on season 16 of DWTS. She was partnered with Derek Hough, and notably beat out Zendaya for the top spot in the competition.

In a recent development, marking the second time Derek Hough won consecutive seasons, Amber Riley was the show’s 17th winner. The Glee star and Derek had quite the impressive turn, tying the then-record for the highest first week score, receiving three nines from the judges. In total, she had five perfect scores throughout the season, which led her to nab the season 17 champion title.

Riley is also notably the first African American woman to win a regular, mainstay season of DWTS. (Melissa Rycroft won All-Stars.).

It has been revealed that olympic silver medalist Meryl Davis nabbed the DWTS mirrorball in 2014 alongside Makism Chmerkovskiy. She notably competed against her ice skating partner Charlie White, who placed fifth. At the time, she broke the record for the most perfect scored dances, with six.

According to recent reports, long before he became a co-host of DWTS, Alfonso Ribeiro won the show in 2014. Earning Witney Carson her first mirrorball as well, the duo were a force during the 19th installment. He matched Amber Riley’s record for best first week score ever, after earning 36/40 (meaning he received four nines from each judge).

Industry observers note that rumer Willis won the landmark 20th season of the competitive ballroom show alongside Valentin Chmerkovskiy, in his first win ever. Daughter to Demi Moore and Bruce Willis, Rumer matched Meryl Davis’ score of most perfect dances by a competitor.

Sources indicate that one of the most heartwrenching journeys on DWTS came with Bindi Irwin’s season 21 appearance with her partner Derek Hough. Son of the beloved Steve Irwin, Bindi was the first winner to completely blow out the once-set record of most perfect dances. Jennifer Grey and Rumer Willis each had six, though Bindi earned eight perfect scores.

During Most Memorable Year week, she paid tribute to her late father with a touching contemporary that is ingrained in DWTS history. Competing on the show in 2015, her younger brother Robert Irwin later joined the show, partaking in season 34 of the series in 2025, exactly 10 years post-her tenure in the competition. After his win, they became the first sibling duo to both win DWTS.

Nyle DiMarco had a historic run during season 22 of DWTS, becoming the first deaf person to win the series. Hailing from one of the final cycles of America’s Next Top Model, DiMarco and Peta Murgatroyd’s time on the competitive reality show broke down barriers.

Sources indicate that another gymnast to be crowned a mirrorball champion, Laurie Hernandez won season 23 with Valentin Chmerkovskiy. She is the youngest DWTS winner ever, as she won the show when she was a mere 16-years-old in 2016.

Industry observers note that rashad Jennings is the fourth NFL player to win DWTS. He won with Emma Slater, marking her first and only win as a pro dancer in 2017.

Jordan Fisher and Lindsay Arnold won the show during 2017’s fall season. Fisher’s time on DWTS was record-breaking, as he notably earned nine perfect scores throughout season 25, taking over Bindi Irwin’s achievement of eight.

In a recent development, olympic bronze medalist Adam Rippon won the first and only season of DWTS: Athletes. Sporting a cast of (you guessed it) only athletes, season 26 was a condensed, four-week installment that saw Jenna Johnson win her first mirrorball.

Industry observers note that bobby Bones’ DWTS win is one of the most controversial conquests in the show’s 20 year run. Dancing with his partner Sharna Burgess, the radio host had the lowest judges scores of the finalists during season 27. His win caused a shift in the DWTS universe — one that signified that viewers’ votes could successfully influence a celebrity to win a show without having the scoring to back it up.

Hannah Brown became the second Bachelorette to appear on DWTS during season 28, and the first to win, with her partner Alan Bersten, marking his first and only win.

Following directly behind her fellow franchise leader, Kaitlyn Bristowe won DWTS during the show’s first season set in the middle of the COVID-19 pandemic. In the fall of 2020, Bristowe earned the title of being the second Bachelorette to earn the mirrorball with her partner Artem Chigvintsev.

It has been revealed that iman Shumpert reigned supreme during another milestone season of DWTS. On season 30, he earned the title of the first NBA star to win the show, also earning Daniella Karagach’s first mirrorball.

Sources indicate that longtime DWTS champion pro Mark Ballas made his grand return to the ballroom after six installments off for an impressive season-long run with Charli D’Amelio. The first TikTok star to join the franchise’s cast, Charli earned six perfect scores during her run on the show. She is also a part of the first duo of non-spousal family members to compete on DWTS, as her mother, Heidi D’Amelio, also appeared on season 31.

It has been revealed that xochitl Gomez won the mirrorball trophy in the fall of 2023. She was partnered with Valentin Chmerkovskiy, notably standing as one of the youngest winners of the show, as she was 17 when she snatched the title.

Joey Graziadei is the most recent winner of DWTS, and the only Bachelor to ever win the competitive ballroom series. He was partnered with Jenna Johnson, totaling her number of wins up to two.

Robert Irwin and Witney Carson won the coveted mirrorball of DWTS‘ 2025 installment, putting a cap on one of the show’s most popular seasons ever. Following in the footsteps of his sister, Robert’s win extended the Irwin family’s impact on the competitive ballroom dance series. Plus, they are the only pair of siblings to both win DWTS.

Ezra Frech was named the winner of Dancing With the Stars season 35 alongside Daniella Karagach, making him the first amputee winner of the series. He is also now the youngest male winner of the series at 21. Their win also marks Daniella’s second mirrorball trophy.

#93432. A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1826 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it.
  • In a recent development, researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger.
  • Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a upcoming lease on life.

In a recent development, researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

In a recent development, "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," said Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a newly introduced paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.".

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion.

In a recent development, for thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Industry observers note that once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly quickly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

It has been revealed that "We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," mentioned co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!".

According to recent reports, scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," remarked co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Latest York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.".

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome.

This kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

It has been revealed that as the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

It has been revealed that but such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

These surviving systems are vital because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb.

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

Industry observers note that the simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao.".

In a recent development, "It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," said co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

In a recent development, the researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

Further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Significant Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De said.

The merger has left astronomers with another vital question: What is Bao like now?

The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs.

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Recent findings suggest that although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

The researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.).

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

Earlier records revealed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) indicated further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another notable development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

It has been revealed that the telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

Scientists promptly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable fresh measurements.

Industry observers note that webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A Upcoming Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars.

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an notable advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

Sources indicate that that timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

According to recent reports, one of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar remarked.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's the latest Angel Studios "great man" biography: a paint-by-numbers storybook drama that treats the audience like it's 10 years old.

Sources indicate that angel Studios, in its quest to deliver movies that remind us of The Way America Used To Be, has brought back the “great man” biography — not so much the old-fashioned Hollywood biopic but, rather, movies like “Young Washington” and “Hershey,” the sort of life-of-the-plaster-saint sagas you used to read in the fifth grade. These are history-based tales that are proud in their simplicity, that abolish all shades of gray, that are intended to inspire but also work on the audience because they’re so comforting. It feels good, in a certain super-square regressive way, to watch a movie about the man who popularized the American chocolate bar and was a paragon of philanthropic generosity besides. At “Hershey,” you feel like you’re 10 years old again, which is both a virtue and not. The film is a paint-by-numbers storybook biopic for the chocolate-loving child in us all — or, maybe, for an audience the movie treats as if it needed its hand held. Related Stories 'Grey's Anatomy' Texas Spinoff Casts 'How to Get Away With Murder' Alum Karla Souza in Lead Role ABC Schedule: 'High Potential' Season 3 Sets January Premiere, 'The Bachelor' Season 30 Debuts in March and More.

Sources indicate that early on, there’s a scene that gives you that kid-in-a-candy-store feeling, because it’s all about…a kid in a candy store. Milton Hershey, played as a boy by James Kelly, has moved with his stern 19th-century Mennonite family from a dairy farm in Pennsylvania Dutch country to the bustling city of Lancaster. There, he wanders into a candy shop, where he’s welcomed by the owner and chief candy maker, played with a touch of screwball carny fervor by Richard Kind. “There’s no sweeter way to make a living,” he claims, offering the boy a candy called a sugar-plum swirl and then taking him under his wing as an apprentice. Milton learns the art of candy, and it’s not long before the film cuts to Philadelphia in 1882, where the adult Milton now has his own candy store with a handsome green-and-white awning.

According to recent reports, he makes hard candy and yummy taffy, but his specialty is caramel bonbons, which he crafts with a special milk recipe. It’s the milk that gives it that luscious velvet smoothness. Milton has got the goods, and he’s a charismatic candy man besides. Finn Wittock, a veteran of Ryan Murphy series (and also “La La Land” and Mike Nichols’s 2012 stage revival of “Death of a Salesman”), is a likable actor who suggests a cross between Orson Welles and Robert Wagner. He’s got a sonorous elegance and gleaming eyes, but with a user-friendly nice-guy veneer. For Milton, making candy is a mission, but he starts off as a faltering businessman; his shop goes under, and that will happen to him again, as he struggles to find an audience for his goodies. Salvation comes in the form of a British aristocrat (Mark Ashworth) who tastes one of Milton’s caramels and puts in an order for 3,000 of them to be shipped to England for a party.

It has been revealed that “Hershey” is a movie in which the hero has obstacles (like his unscrupulous candy-business rival), but no demons or inner conflicts. He’s just like his candies: sweet on the outside and the inside. For a while, caramel is king, but it’s chocolate that’s the future. The film colors in the period when Milton is leveraged up to his eyeballs and still searching for the perfect recipe; he figures out that milk is the key here as well. But the aspect of Milton Hershey the movie is actually most interested in is that he popularized what had formerly been elite candy. The Swiss and British chocolates that inspire him are all based on secret recipes, and they’re so expensive that few can afford them. Hershey wants to make a great candy bar that will sell for five cents, so anybody can buy one. He pays his workers top dollar and gives them shares in the tech giant. He’s a turn-of-the-century Willy Wonka as utopian socialist dreamer.

Recent findings suggest that wittrock makes Hershey appealingly robust in his chocolate passion, and that drew me into the movie. What kept nudging me out of it was how sketchy it is. “Hershey” was directed by Mark Waters, who did lively work in the late ’90s and 2000s (“Mean Girls,” “The House of Yes”), but here he skitters through a script that’s so perfunctory it treats even the invention of the Hershey’s Kiss as just one more oh-and-this-happened incident. The dew-drop-shaped candy first results from a faulty machine, but we never see Milton — or anyone else — rhapsodize about it, sharing with the audience what makes it so special. (They never even mention the silver-foil wrapping.) My own theory of the Hershey’s Kiss is that it’s a magical candy because it’s made of the very same chocolate as a Hershey bar, yet that succulent shape somehow makes it taste different.

Industry observers note that milton meets and marries the feisty Kitty (Alexandra Daddario), who loves him, spars affectionately with him, and inspires him to establish a school for impoverished children. But the desire to move back to his old homestead and build an entire town in Pennsylvania Dutch country — the factory town of Hershey, which will be part workers’ paradise, part Disneyland — is his own. They’re living the dream until Kitty starts to succumb to muscle seizures, and it turns out she has a degenerative illness, progressive paraplegia. The movie refuses to characterize her condition as tragic, but it does use it to inspire what we might call faith-based tears.

According to recent reports, “Hershey” is a movie that makes you hungry for chocolate, and that’s part of its appeal. So is the notion that a legendary American entrepreneur could ever have been this much of a selfless gentleman. Yet the movie simulates your sweet tooth without necessarily satisfying it. Chocolate, as anyone who craves it knows, is no casual delight. There’s something orgasmic about chocolate (yes, even a Hershey bar), but in “Hershey” it’s a strictly civilized pleasure.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (358 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another.
  • According to recent reports, the image demonstrates the Didymos double asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos.
  • It has been revealed that the image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another.

According to recent reports, the image demonstrates the Didymos double asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos.

It has been revealed that the image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system.

Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth.

For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth.

But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid, meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet.

Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

#93427. Latest Update: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1922 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Hundreds of millions at risk from Chinese shopping app malware

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.
  • But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass owners’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.
  • While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is one of China’s most popular shopping apps, selling clothing, groceries and just about everything else under the sun to more than 750 million users a month.

But according to cybersecurity researchers, it can also bypass owners’ cell phone security to monitor activities on other apps, check notifications, read private messages and change settings.

And once installed, it’s tough to remove.

While many apps collect vast troves of user data, sometimes without explicit consent, experts say e-commerce giant Pinduoduo has taken violations of privacy and data security to the next level.

In a detailed investigation, CNN spoke to half a dozen cybersecurity teams from Asia, Europe and the United States — as well as multiple former and current Pinduoduo employees — after receiving a tipoff.

Multiple experts identified the presence of malware on the Pinduoduo app that exploited vulnerabilities in Android operating systems. Company insiders mentioned the exploits were utilized to spy on users and competitors, allegedly to boost sales.

“We haven’t seen a mainstream app like this trying to escalate their privileges to gain access to things that they’re not supposed to gain access to,” said Mikko Hyppönen, chief research officer at WithSecure, a Finnish cybersecurity firm.

“This is highly unusual, and it is pretty damning for Pinduoduo.”.

Malware, short for malicious software, refers to any software developed to steal data or interfere with computer systems and mobile devices.

Evidence of sophisticated malware in the Pinduoduo app comes amid intense scrutiny of Chinese-developed apps like TikTok over concerns about data security.

Some American lawmakers are pushing for a national ban on the popular short-video app, whose CEO Shou Chew was grilled by Congress for five hours last week about its relations with the Chinese government.

Industry observers note that the revelations are also likely to draw more attention to Pinduoduo’s international sister app, Temu, which is topping US download charts and fast expanding in other Western markets. Both are owned by Nasdaq-listed PDD, a multinational company with roots in China.

While Temu has not been implicated, Pinduoduo’s alleged actions risk casting a shadow over its sister app’s global expansion.

There is no evidence that Pinduoduo has handed data to the Chinese government. But as Beijing enjoys significant leverage over businesses under its jurisdiction, there are concerns from US lawmakers that any manufacturer operating in China could be forced to cooperate with a broad range of security activities.

The findings follow Google’s suspension of Pinduoduo from its Play Store in March, citing malware identified in versions of the app.

An ensuing report from Bloomberg noted a Russian cybersecurity firm had also identified potential malware in the app.

Pinduoduo has previously rejected “the speculation and accusation that Pinduoduo app is malicious.”.

CNN has contacted PDD multiple times over email and phone for comment, but has not received a response.

Pinduoduo, which boasts a user base that accounts for three quarters of China’s online population and a market value three times that of eBay (EBAY), wasn’t always an online shopping behemoth.

Founded in 2015 in Shanghai by Colin Huang, a former Google employee, the startup was fighting to establish itself in a market long dominated by e-commerce stalwarts Alibaba (BABA) and JD.com (JD).

It succeeded by offering steep discounts on friends-and-family group buying orders and focusing on lower-income rural areas.

According to recent reports, pinduoduo posted triple digit growth in monthly owners until the end of 2018, the year it listed in Fresh York. By the middle of 2020, though, the increase in monthly users had slowed to around 50% and would continue to decline, according to its earnings reports.

It was in 2020, according to a current Pinduoduo employee, that the manufacturer set up a team of about 100 engineers and product managers to dig for vulnerabilities in Android phones, develop ways to exploit them — and turn that into profit.

According to the source, who requested anonymity for fear of reprisals, the company only targeted consumers in rural areas and smaller towns initially, while avoiding users in megacities such as Beijing and Shanghai.

“The goal was to reduce the risk of being exposed,” they said.

By collecting expansive data on user activities, the organization was able to create a comprehensive portrait of users’ habits, interests and preferences, according to the source.

This allowed it to improve its machine learning model to offer more personalized push notifications and ads, attracting customers to open the app and place orders, they said.

The team was disbanded in early March, the source added, after questions about their activities came to light.

PDD didn’t reply to CNN’s repeated requests for comment on the team.

Approached by CNN, researchers from Tel Aviv-based cyber firm Check Point Research, Delaware-based app security startup Oversecured and Hyppönen’s WithSecure conducted independent analysis of the 6.49.0 version of the app, released on Chinese app stores in late February.

Google Play is not available in China, and Android people in the country download their apps from local stores. In March, when Google suspended Pinduoduo, it noted it had found malware in off-Play versions of the app.

The researchers found code designed to achieve “privilege escalation”: a type of cyberattack that exploits a vulnerable operating system to gain a higher level of access to data than it’s supposed to have, according to experts.

“Our team has reverse engineered that code and we can confirm that it tries to escalate rights, tries to gain access to things normal apps wouldn’t be able to do on Android phones,” stated Hyppönen.

In a recent development, the app was able to continue running in the background and prevent itself from being uninstalled, which allowed it to boost its monthly active user rates, Hyppönen noted. It also had the ability to spy on competitors by tracking activity on other shopping apps and getting information from them, he added.

Check Point Research additionally identified ways in which the app was able to evade scrutiny.

The app deployed a method that allowed it to push updates without an app store review process meant to detect malicious applications, the researchers said.

They also identified in some plug-ins the intent to obscure potentially malicious components by hiding them under legitimate file names, such as Google’s.

“Such a technique is widely used by malware developers that inject malicious code into applications that have legitimate functionality,” they said.

In China, about three quarters of smartphone consumers are on the Android system. Apple (AAPL)’s iPhone has 25% market share, according to Daniel Ives of Wedbush Securities.

Sergey Toshin, the founder of Oversecured, noted Pinduoduo’s malware specifically targeted different Android-based operating systems, including those used by Samsung, Huawei, Xiaomi and Oppo.

CNN has reached out to these companies for comment.

Toshin described Pinduoduo as “the most dangerous malware” ever found among mainstream apps.

Sources indicate that “I’ve never seen anything like this before. It’s like, super expansive,” he said.

Most phone manufacturers globally customize the core Android software, the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), to add unique features and applications to their own devices.

It has been revealed that toshin found Pinduoduo to have exploited about 50 Android system vulnerabilities. Most of the exploits were tailor made for customized parts known as the original equipment manufacturer (OEM) code, which tends to be audited less often than AOSP and is therefore more prone to vulnerabilities, he stated.

Recent findings suggest that pinduoduo also exploited a number of AOSP vulnerabilities, including one which was flagged by Toshin to Google in February 2022. Google fixed the bug this March, he remarked.

Industry observers note that according to Toshin, the exploits allowed Pinduoduo access to people’ locations, contacts, calendars, notifications and photo albums without their consent. They were also able to change system settings and access users’ social network accounts and chats, he remarked.

Of the six teams CNN spoke to for this story, three did not conduct full examinations. But their primary reviews revealed that Pinduoduo asked for a large number of permissions beyond the normal functions of a shopping app.

They included “potentially invasive permissions” such as “set wallpaper” and “download without notification,” remarked René Mayrhofer, head of the Institute of Networks and Security at the Johannes Kepler University Linz in Austria.

Suspicions about malware in Pinduoduo’s app were first raised in late February in a report by a Chinese cybersecurity firm called Dark Navy. Even though the analysis didn’t directly name the shopping giant, the report spread quickly among other researchers, who did name the company. Some of the analysts followed up with their own reports confirming the original findings.

Soon after, on March 5, Pinduoduo issued a latest upgrade of its app, version 6.50.0, which removed the exploits, according to two experts who CNN spoke to.

Two days after the patch, Pinduoduo disbanded the team of engineers and product managers who had developed the exploits, according to the Pinduoduo source.

Industry observers note that the next day, team members found themselves locked out of Pinduoduo’s bespoke workplace communication app, Knock, and lost access to files on the manufacturer’s internal network. Engineers also found their access to major data, data sheets and the log system revoked, the source stated.

Sources indicate that most of the team were transferred to work at Temu. They were assigned to different departments at the subsidiary, with some working on marketing or developing push notifications, according to the source.

A core group of about 20 cybersecurity engineers who specialize in finding and exploiting vulnerabilities remain at Pinduoduo, they said.

Toshin of Oversecured, who looked into the enhancement, stated although the exploits were removed, the underlying code was still there and could be reactivated to carry out attacks.

Pinduoduo has been able to grow its user base against a backdrop of the Chinese government’s regulatory clampdown on Big Tech that began in late 2020.

That year, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology launched a sweeping crackdown on apps that illegally collect and use personal data.

In 2021, Beijing passed its first comprehensive data privacy legislation.

The Personal Information Protection Law stipulates that no party should illegally collect, process or transmit personal information. They’re also banned from exploiting internet-related security vulnerabilities or engaging in actions that endanger cybersecurity.

Pinduoduo’s apparent malware would be a violation of those laws, tech policy experts say, and should have been detected by the regulator.

“This would be embarrassing for the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, because this is their job,” noted Kendra Schaefer, a tech policy expert at Trivium China, a consultancy. “They’re supposed to check Pinduoduo, and the fact that they didn’t find (anything) is embarrassing for the regulator.”.

The ministry has regularly published lists to name and shame apps found to have undermined user privacy or other rights. It also publishes a separate list of apps that are removed from app stores for failing to comply with regulations.

Pinduoduo did not appear on any of the lists.

CNN has reached out to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and the Cyberspace Administration of China for comment.

On Chinese social media, some cybersecurity experts questioned why regulators haven’t taken any action.

Industry observers note that “Probably none of our regulators can understand coding and programming, nor do they understand technology. You can’t even understand the malicious code when it’s shoved right in front of your face,” a cybersecurity expert with 1.8 million followers wrote last week in a viral post on Weibo, a Twitter-like platform.

The post was censored the next day.

CNN’s Kristie Lu Stout and Sean Lyngaas contributed reporting.

Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen.
  • Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility.
  • Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

Quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.

Sources indicate that now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times.".

According to recent reports, atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A Latest Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times.

The researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

Recent findings suggest that "It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a newly introduced technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.".

That improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A Newly introduced Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity.

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

Sources indicate that for now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

"Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the major next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.".

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

Tech Report: How cautious investors are struggling to avoid the AI bubble

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.
  • After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.
  • The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index roared back to life this week after a worrying sell-off recently that saw huge falls in technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-related stocks.

After suffering its worst week since the pandemic crash of March 2020, the Nasdaq opened Monday (November 23) nearly 1,700 points, or 7%, higher.

The AI trade received a further boost after Nvidia reinstated CEO Jensen Huang on Monday, just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid a scandal involving extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

The chipmaker's stock rose more than 30% on the news, opening at nearly $170 (€155.5) per share and recovering most of the losses since last month, when the affair was first reported.

The surge helped propel US stock indices to their best day since last year. But in premarket trading on Tuesday, Nvidia fell about 5%, underscoring the volatility of the market and the risks facing the AI sector and the broader tech industry.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The recent volatility around AI, memory chips and other technology stocks has unnerved even the most experienced and bullish investors.

Yet, those seeking a haven away from the United States stock market, which has enjoyed the majority of the AI hype — along with Taiwan and South Korea — are increasingly finding few places to shelter.

Economists warn that this is partly due to the way index funds, including exchange-traded funds (ETFs), work. These funds hold the pensions and other savings of hundreds of millions of passive investors.

These indices have become increasingly exposed to the AI boom.

According to recent reports, most flagship index funds are keen to ride winners, so they automatically buy stocks according to a organization's market value. The bigger a company grows, the more of it they hold.

The values of Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other US technology giants have benefited from this effect, with many soaring after ChatGPT was first released in late 2022.

It has been revealed that the US also has an outsized position in funds that track the global economy. Nine of the top 10 holdings of the MSCI All Country World Index (ACWI), an index of more than 2,400 firms across 47 developed and emerging markets, are US Substantial Tech names.

The other is TSMC, a Taiwanese chipmaker that produces 90% of the high-end AI semiconductors.

Together, these 10 holdings make up nearly a quarter of the index.

Although it's a global index, nearly two-thirds of MSCI ACWI's value is in US-listed companies, even though they make up only around a fifth of its firms.

"A well-diversified portfolio should ... reasonably represent the entire global economy," Gerd Kommer, founder of the Munich-based asset manager Gerd Kommer Invest, told DW.

"That's not the case if 70% of the portfolio is concentrated in just one country — the US. The global economy is more resilient than any national economy.".

Kommer, who is known as Germany's "ETF pope," remarked investors need exposure to all economic sectors and that no single sector should make up more than a quarter of a portfolio.

Yet, even if investors want to avoid US-dominated World funds altogether, the AI trade still overshadows several other top index funds.

Sources indicate that in MSCI's Emerging Market index, for example, the top 10 make up 37.5% of its value and TSMC alone accounts for almost 16%. Tech, chip and internet firms make up eight of the largest holdings, alongside two banks — one Chinese, one Indian.

That matters, according to Dimitri Vayanos, a finance professor at the London School of Economics who studies how passive investing pushes up the prices of the biggest firms.

"My model suggests that the effects of flows into index funds are larger when the large stocks happen to be in the same industry," Vayanos told DW.

When some investors get over-optimistic about a firm and push the stock price up, index funds add to that price pressure.

In a recent development, professional investors then often bet against overpriced stocks, a practice known as "shorting," which helps pull prices back down. But that's far riskier with, say, a tech giant than with a small firm.

"Being short 1% of SpaceX involves much more risk than being short 1% of a small tech giant," noted Vayanos.

In a recent development, the problem gets worse when the biggest firms are all in the same sector, as they are now. As short-sellers hold back, the biggest stocks climb further, creating what he calls an "amplification-overpricing spiral.".

According to recent reports, to cut exposure to AI-related stocks, investors may have to turn to developed market funds outside the US and Southeast Asia. These funds have offered lower returns over the past decade.

In the MSCI Europe, Australasia and Far East (EAFE) index fund, the top 10 holdings make up about 14.5% of the index, about 40% lower than the all-country world index.

EAFE's major holdings include healthcare giant Roche, oil major Shell, HSBC bank and Nestle — the world's largest food and beverage tech giant.

However, its biggest holding, ASML, is still very much part of the AI trade. The Dutch tech firm sells the equipment that firms such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK Hynix and Micron need to make their chips.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If Monday's rebound in the AI trade is sustained, stock prices may move sharply higher over the next few months. Yet if history is a guide, the bubble will eventually burst, leaving both institutional and passive investors nursing heavy losses.

Kommer warned that if the AI bubble bursts, "in all likelihood it will drag down the global stock market," though the damage would be most severe in tech and AI stocks.

Those hit hardest would be retail investors "with heavy portfolio weights in tech and AI stocks," he remarked, including "a lot of people who have bought individual AI-related stocks on top of their equity ETFs.".

LSE's Vayanos thinks it is still "certainly safer to hold an ETF than to hold individual stocks.".

But as index providers add mega-IPOs such as SpaceX and Claude-maker Anthropic to benchmarks within weeks of their debut, and money continues to pour into passive funds, he warned that "the conditions are present for the effects of our theory to be even stronger.".
