Lowe's on Wednesday posted strong quarterly results and raised its full-year outlook as the manufacturer remarked it saw strength among professional shoppers.

Sources indicate that the company remarked comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.

Because of the strength, Lowe's now noted it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.

CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the tech giant is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He said Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years.

"We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.

In a recent development, lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the firm intends to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.

He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects.

"We are giving those pros what they need," he said. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program.".

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

It has been revealed that for the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.

Industry observers note that the home improvement retailer has previously said it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The manufacturer is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates.

Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year.

Lowe's executives stated on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are right now around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter.

"So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said.

Ellison told CNBC the manufacturer remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far.

Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday.
  • This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report remarked ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.
  • The total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around 47,000 women and girls — or five every hour — were killed by intimate partners or family members in 2025, according to a United Nations report released on Tuesday.

This figure equates to around 60% of women and girls who were victims of intentional homicides last year, the report remarked ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women on November 25.

The total fatalities were calculated based on statistics from 122 countries and territories. They translate to an average of 129 women and girls killed by their close social circle each day.

Africa recorded the highest number of femicides, at 22,100. Asia followed, with 15,100 victims, ahead of the Americas with 7,400, Europe with 2,100 and Oceania with 300.

Femicide is a hate crime broadly defined as "the intentional killing of women or girls because they are female.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The report also found that although global homicide rates have declined, femicide rates have fallen at a slower pace, particularly in the Americas and Europe.

According to the UN, this highlights the barriers women often face in accessing the justice system and that "these crimes are deeply rooted in social norms and gender stereotypes.".

Nearly one in three women worldwide have experienced physical or sexual violence, yet only 7% reported it to the police, a separate UN Women report found.

According to estimates by UN Women and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC, the number of women and girls killed by a family member or an intimate partner has wavered between 45,000 and 51,000 over the past several years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that "Frightening attitudes, social norms, and the failure of institutional safeguards create an environment in which killing a wife, daughter, mother, or sister becomes 'tolerable,'" UNODC director Monica Juma mentioned. "Changing this reality calls for sustained action across all levels of society.".

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, mentioned that the world needed to "act urgently to ensure no warning sign is ignored, no survivor is left without protection, and no perpetrator escapes accountability.".

Breaking: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System.
  • It has been revealed that latest research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed.
  • The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide key clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

It has been revealed that latest research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Vital Clues.

Dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

Recent findings suggest that "The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan said.

Industry observers note that "Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth.".

Recent findings suggest that "By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment.".

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts.

Industry observers note that to investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

These findings offer a upcoming perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

The implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth.

In a recent development, "The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan said.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a upcoming era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side.".

The return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.

Materials provided by Curtin University. Original written by Lucien Wilkinson. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov.
  • It has been revealed that this dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K.
  • Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

It has been revealed that this dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

Recent findings suggest that "When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over.".

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so newly introduced fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion.".

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey.".

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

It has been revealed that "You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”.

It has been revealed that "Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

Sources indicate that encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The company also said it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

In a recent development, "The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time.".

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the manufacturer performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Sources indicate that for the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

This year, the organization said it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

The tech giant stated it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength showed "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

The massive-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and remarked it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

According to recent reports, it's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer said on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

However, rather than focusing on a sad orphan in England, Hexed's Potter-like tale centers on the Ohio-raised daughter of a mother whose love language is smothering.

This combination mixes the coming-of-age comedy and mother-daughter drama of Turning Red with a magical realm reminiscent of Harry Potter (and the underrated Disney show Owl House), creating an entertaining elixir that's fun, imaginative, and moving.

Hailee Steinfeld lends her voice to Billie Doe, a teen girl introduced through a heist in which she steals her high school's mascot (a befuddled owl) so he can be set free. This seemingly bad behavior — which includes "borrowing" her mom's car without a driver's license — is more than an act of rebellion against school uniforms, her grumbling principal (Brett Gelman), or her overprotective mother, Alice (Rashida Jones). Scored by Queen's rapturous anthem "I Want to Break Free," it's a symbolic act that plays as this Disney heroine's "I wish" song, though this Disney heroine doesn't get an original song of her own. Billie wants to be free to spread her wings and be herself.

For years, Billie's mother has given her endless "guidelines," building around her a world of rules from which Billie is desperate to escape. So, when a magical portal opens in her bedroom, of course she rushes on through without looking back. But this won't be a story where Billie pulls a Dorothy Gale in Oz, wandering around alone while her mother figure Auntie Em is none the wiser. Shortly after Billie has tumbled into the magical realm of Hexe and made a spectacle out of herself by flying with style, her mother Alice follows.

In a recent development, together, they will battle against the vicious Queen Celeste (Jodie Foster), and her fleet of half-raven/half-human Morphlings. (Imagine if the Wicked Witch's flying monkeys were chic, side-eyeing goth girls with shapeshifting abilities). But to join forces, they first have to understand each other, literally traveling into each other's minds to see each other's perspectives. That's a bit of magic we could all use.

In a recent development, bound to Billie, we're promptly made aware that she doesn't fit in. A school photo indicates her not only off in the corner with a glum look on her face as the other kids smile in unison, but also with more vibrantly colored hair and skin that sets her apart. She's not regarded as beautiful for this, but strange and worthy of shunning.

Sources indicate that she loves plants, attracts stray cats, and possesses a reckless streak that makes her one of the rowdiest Disney heroines since The Little Mermaid. And while her classmates might scoff and her teachers might sneer, Billie is dedicated to being herself. But when her mother sneers at her, she almost literally shrinks.

Industry observers note that it hurts to believe your mother sees you as a screw-up. This major feeling becomes a crucial incentive for three of the film's lead characters, having sprawling consequences. Maybe we can't choose to not be hurt by a parent's rejection. But we can choose how we respond. Will we cave to their pressure? Will we dull our own shine or corrupt our hearts to distort ourselves to meet their expectations? Or will we soar above?

It has been revealed that the plotline of mothers and teen daughters struggling to see each other outside of the parenthood dynamic puts Hexed on the same path as Brave and Turning Red. In each of these Disney animated films, the mother seems cold as she urges her daughter to assimilate to societal norms. But in each instance, it's with the goal of protecting her from hardship.

Sources indicate that however, Hexed gives deeper space to the idea that being forced to be like everyone else by the very person who should believe you are special is its own kind of hell. And it's not one invented with each new generation, but a trauma that can reach back, scarring those who come after.

In a recent development, for this intense central drama and all its macabre elements, Hexed is nonstop entertaining. Steinfeld recaptures the teen angst and rebellious spirit she showed in the phenomenal live-action coming-of-age comedy The Edge of Seventeen. Jones brings her wry wit to Alice, while Foster's sharpness cuts like a knife through velvet. You can practically hear her targets' self-esteem being shredded to ribbons.

Industry observers note that while there's plenty of noteworthy names in the ensemble cast, including Dan Stevens, Tracey Ullman, Randall Park, Stephen Fry, and Henry Winkler, it's Fallout's Walton Goggins who proves an unrepentant scene-stealer. Slathering on a Cajun accent like it's barbecue sauce, Goggins brings a surly but sweet attitude to a three-eyed cat familiar named Beef Roger Crummchuk. If that name alone has you intrigued, you'll love Hexed. Chaotic, intriguing, and silly, this character's name is a solid distillation of the movie itself. Plus, Goggins and Steinfeld have terrific chemistry as an overeager protégé and a wizened mentor.

The filmmakers have bypassed the typically clean Disney aesthetic, which demands its heroines be soft, round, and always pretty, and worked in some alt elements to give Billie an easy-to-clock baby goth look. In a beautiful and meaningful element of the movie's color story, the teals and fuchsias that Billie favors in her Ohio life are reflected in Hexe, along with golds and purples that all suggest she belongs, as she visually fits in this world she's never known. But when it comes to the colors of the queen, they are chillier, more muted, speaking not only to the difference between heroine and villainess, but also to the distinction in their energies.

Recent findings suggest that with a spirited sense of humor and a pop music soundtrack, Hexed brings an inviting verve to its story of generational trauma. And in that, it helps the spoonful of medicine go down, for the children and parents in the audience alike. For those kids not old enough to be having this kind of psychological connection to Hexed, they'll be delighted with the daffy physical humor, rousing action sequences, and an array of colorful characters who'll frighten and delight. Hexed is spell-binding.

A galactic shock wave could rewrite the map of the Milky Way

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Fresh research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas.
  • Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh research suggests the Milky Way produces stars in an unexpected location, revealing a surprising difference between our galaxy and most of its neighbors. The findings also raise questions about a familiar feature of the Milky Way, suggesting that part of what astronomers have long considered a spiral arm may actually be something else.

Industry observers note that the discovery comes from research led by a University of Sydney PhD student, who found evidence that a massive rotating structure of stars near the galactic center is generating powerful shock waves through surrounding clouds of gas. These waves squeeze the gas together, creating conditions that allow newly introduced stars to form in a region where such intense forces usually prevent their birth.

Published in Nature Astronomy, the study also casts doubt on the nature of the Norma spiral arm, a feature of the Milky Way named for the constellation Norma as seen from Earth.

Lead author Dr. Hillary Davis, who recently completed her PhD at the University of Sydney's School of Physics and Sydney Institute for Astronomy, remarked the research provides newly introduced insights into the structures near the galactic center and how gas moves around them.

"At its heart, star formation is a process we understand from everyday physics. Forces set matter in motion. In this case gas is compressed, and that compression can create the conditions for new stars to be born on a massive scale," Dr. Davis noted.

In a recent development, "In most similar galaxies, star formation very commonly occurs along spiral arms. What's extraordinary is seeing this happen in a different region of our Galaxy, where shocks are usually so strong that star formation is often suppressed.".

A Hidden Star Factory at the Heart of the Milky Way.

Recent findings suggest that the Milky Way belongs to a class of galaxies known as barred spiral galaxies. Unlike galaxies with only a central concentration of stars and surrounding spiral arms, these systems contain an elongated structure of stars stretching across their central region. In our galaxy, this structure is called the Galactic bar.

According to recent reports, as the bar rotates, its gravity influences nearby gas, driving it into powerful shock fronts. These fronts compress the gas in much the same way that a shock wave compresses air.

Studying this structure from Earth is particularly difficult because we are located inside the Milky Way rather than viewing it from the outside. Large amounts of cosmic dust also block our view of the galactic center.

"The Galactic bar cannot be easily observed because of a combination of our position in the Galaxy and dust obscuring our view," Dr. Davis remarked.

"As a result, the bar's properties have been highly debated.".

Observations of other barred galaxies have shown that these shock fronts generally inhibit the formation of new stars, even in regions containing abundant gas. The intense conditions make it difficult for the gas to collapse into stars.

According to recent reports, however, the fresh findings indicate that the Milky Way may behave differently. Although it is not the only known example, our galaxy appears to belong to a relatively small group in which substantial star formation takes place along the shock fronts of the central bar.

"We believe that the Milky Way's bar has star formation occurring along its shock front, which is uncommon for most bars in nearby galaxies," Dr. Davis said.

A Milky Way Spiral Arm May Not Be What It Seems.

To investigate this unusual activity, the research team compared detailed computer simulations showing how galaxies change over billions of years with astronomical observations of regions where massive stars are forming.

A crucial part of the evidence came from masers, naturally occurring sources that emit highly concentrated microwave radiation. These emissions are associated with the formation of massive stars and operate on a principle similar to lasers, but at microwave wavelengths.

By examining the positions of these masers, the researchers uncovered a striking match between actual observations and the locations of shock fronts predicted by their simulations.

In a recent development, "We found that masers previously associated with the Norma arm closely align with the shock front predicted by our simulations," Dr. Davis said. "This suggests that at least part of the so-called Norma arm may not be a spiral arm at all, but a region of star formation along the leading edge of the Galactic bar.

"This raises questions about the Galaxy's spiral structure, and the bar region of the Milky Way, which needs further investigation," she remarked.

According to recent reports, the possibility is significant because it suggests that some of the star formation previously attributed to the Norma spiral arm could instead be occurring along the central bar. If confirmed, this interpretation would change how astronomers understand the arrangement of stars and gas in that part of the Milky Way.

New Evidence Could Redraw the Milky Way's Map.

Beyond revealing an unusual location for star birth, the research also sheds light on the physical properties of the Galactic bar itself.

Astronomers have debated the structure's length, orientation, and rotation speed for decades, partly because the Milky Way's dust and our viewing position make direct measurements so challenging.

According to recent reports, "Our findings place further constraints on the size, angle and rotation speed of this central bar," Dr. Davis said.

In a recent development, the team's analysis indicates that the bar extends approximately 4.3 kiloparsecs, equivalent to about 14,000 light-years, outward from the galactic center along its long axis. This supports a picture of the Milky Way containing a relatively long bar that rotates slowly.

According to recent reports, the results illustrate how increasingly sophisticated simulations can help scientists investigate regions of our galaxy that are difficult to observe directly. By comparing models spanning billions of years with the available astronomical evidence, researchers can narrow down the possible structures and processes shaping the Milky Way.

"By comparing a new generation of large-scale computerized galaxy simulations, evolving over billions of years, against a more limited set of observations, we now have a stronger understanding of the bar and star formation processes in the Milky Way," Dr. Davis stated.

Recent findings suggest that the authors reported no competing interests. Research funding came from the Australian Research Council, the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation, the Swedish Research Council, the Swedish National Space Agency, the LMK Foundation and eSSENCE (Sweden).

Computing resources and data storage were provided through National Computing Infrastructure Australia, an NCRIS capability supported by the Australian Government, and LUNARC, the Centre for Scientific and Technical Computing at Lund University, Sweden.

#93396. Tech Report: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy releases the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

Tech Report: On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy releases the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.
  • Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.
  • After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were debuted.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was debuted by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds.".

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have introduced since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

#93395. A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1501 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1501 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside.
  • Researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them.
  • Recent findings suggest that their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some of the smallest black holes ever proposed may be capable of destroying entire stars from the inside. Scientists believe these mysterious objects, known as primordial black holes, could have formed during the first fraction of a second after the Significant Bang, when extremely dense regions of matter collapsed under their own gravity. If they exist, these ancient remnants could also account for a substantial portion of dark matter, the invisible material that makes up most of the matter in the universe.

Researchers at MIT and other institutions have now identified a possible way to find them. Using theoretical calculations and computer simulations in three dimensions, the team investigated what would happen if a primordial black hole became trapped inside a star similar to our Sun.

Recent findings suggest that their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal, describes a remarkable possibility. A black hole no larger than an atom, but carrying the mass of an asteroid, could gradually sink toward the center of a star and begin consuming it from within.

If the star rotates rapidly enough, material falling toward the black hole would eventually form a spinning disk around it. That development could set the stage for a catastrophic explosion.

"Once the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star," says lead author Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT.

Sources indicate that the interaction between the black hole and the surrounding disk could produce enormous jets of matter that punch through the star and cause it to explode within seconds. Researchers predict that the resulting outburst would emit intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with X-rays and gamma rays, potentially making it visible to telescopes already in operation.

"There is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars," Gottlieb indicates. "We expect this to be visible, and it's something we should look into.".

The research team also included Matteo Cantiello of the Flatiron Institute, Cameron Norton and Matthew Kleban of Fresh York University, and Ken Van Tilburg of Stanford University.

Ancient Black Holes That May Have Survived the Big Bang.

Recent findings suggest that not every primordial black hole formed in the early universe would still exist today. According to a theory developed by physicist Stephen Hawking, black holes gradually lose energy through a quantum process called Hawking radiation. Over immense periods of time, this process causes them to shrink, and the smallest primordial black holes would already have evaporated completely.

Recent findings suggest that heavier primordial black holes, however, could have survived to the present day. Some might be approximately the size of an atom while containing as much mass as an asteroid (or about a millionth of the mass of the Earth).

These extraordinary objects raise an intriguing question. If they are still scattered throughout the universe, what would happen when one encounters a star? More importantly, could the resulting interaction provide the evidence needed to establish that primordial black holes actually exist?

Sources indicate that to investigate, Gottlieb and his colleagues combined mathematical calculations with numerical simulations incorporating general relativity, fluid dynamics, stellar evolution, and particle physics. Their goal was to understand how a primordial black hole could become trapped by a star and what would happen afterward.

How a Tiny Black Hole Could Become Trapped Inside a Star.

The researchers found that a star acting alone generally could not capture a primordial black hole passing nearby. Its gravitational attraction would be insufficient to keep the black hole from escaping.

The situation changes when another object is involved. A companion star or planet could alter the gravitational interaction enough to allow the primordial black hole to become trapped.

Industry observers note that in this arrangement involving three objects, the black hole could repeatedly travel through the star. Each passage would create friction as it moved through stellar material, gradually draining energy from its orbit and drawing it closer to the star's center.

The process could take thousands or even millions of years. Although that sounds extraordinarily slow, it is relatively brief compared with the age of the universe.

Eventually, the black hole would settle into the star's core, where it could begin feeding on the surrounding material.

"Then, this is where the action begins," Gottlieb notes.

A Black Hole Could Slowly Consume a Star From Within.

It has been revealed that once the primordial black hole reaches the stellar core, its growth depends partly on what happens to the energy generated as gas falls toward it. Some of that energy can heat the surrounding material, potentially slowing the rate at which additional gas falls inward.

It has been revealed that the team's simulations indicate that most of the energy would instead disappear into the black hole. This would allow it to accumulate matter more rapidly than earlier estimates suggested.

Industry observers note that over several million years, the growing black hole could consume approximately 1 percent of the star's total mass. At that stage, its fate would depend heavily on how rapidly the star rotates.

In a recent development, if the star spins fast enough, gas would no longer be able to plunge directly into the black hole. Instead, the material would gather into a rotating disk around the black hole, which would by then have grown to several meters in size.

"Inside the star, you have a black hole with a disk," Gottlieb indicates. "The black hole is also spinning, and it's twisting space and time.".

As the disk continues feeding the black hole, the extreme rotation twists the magnetic field threading the surrounding material. This process could generate exceptionally powerful jets that shoot outward from the black hole's poles.

It has been revealed that "This twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole," Gottlieb explains. "And these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds. It's very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.".

What began as a tiny black hole hidden inside an otherwise ordinary star could therefore end in a violent explosion, with the star's destruction unfolding in a matter of seconds once the critical conditions are reached.

Exploding Stars Could Reveal Primordial Black Holes and Dark Matter.

The researchers also calculated what these unusual explosions might look like to astronomers, estimating how their brightness and color would change across different wavelengths of light.

Their models predict a recognizable sequence of emissions, beginning with high-energy radiation and progressing through other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum as the explosion evolves. The initial outburst could include intense blue and ultraviolet light, along with gamma rays and X-rays.

"We would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions," Gottlieb says. "This is something we could potentially detect, if it's not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.".

Such signals could be detectable with existing astronomical instruments, potentially allowing researchers to search for primordial black holes far beyond the Milky Way.

Industry observers note that however, identifying one would not be straightforward. Other cosmic events can generate similar flashes of radiation, so an unusual explosion alone would not establish that a primordial black hole was responsible.

Industry observers note that astronomers would need to examine additional evidence, including the characteristics of the exploding star. One especially revealing clue would be an explosion involving a star that would not ordinarily be expected to meet such a violent end.

In a recent development, "For instance, if the star is a certain mass that is not supposed to explode, it must be something that is happening inside that is a sort of parasite that is consuming the star from the inside," Gottlieb indicates. "The broader impact is that we can now place constraints on primordial black holes, and their contributions to dark matter, using observations.".

Even if no convincing examples are found, the search could help scientists determine how common primordial black holes might be and how much dark matter they could account for.

Sources indicate that for now, primordial black holes remain hypothetical. But the new research offers astronomers a possible observational signature to pursue, connecting the spectacular destruction of stars with objects that may have existed since the universe's earliest moments.

The research received partial support from the U.S. Department of Energy Office of Science Advanced Scientific Computing Research Program and the National Science Foundation.

Hims & Hers rolls out fresh peptide treatments — while admitting there's more to learn about efficacy

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday noted it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S.
  • Even as it confirmed the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.
  • Industry observers note that the new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that hims & Hers Health on Wednesday noted it will offer five formulations of peptides and longevity treatments compounded in the U.S. as part of the initial rollout of its Peptides+ platform, all of which are not approved by regulators.

Even as it confirmed the new products, Hims & Hers acknowledged it has more to learn about how best to use the peptides and how effective they are — underscoring the uncertainty surrounding the growing space.

Industry observers note that the new offerings come after the federal government eased restrictions on compounding certain unapproved peptides, which are short chains of amino ​acids. Those products have exploded in popularity among fitness and longevity enthusiasts who attest that they help with muscle growth, rapid injury recovery and anti-aging, even though most lack evidence from robust human trials.

Hims in late October launched an early access list for the upcoming peptide offerings, and more than 10,000 people signed up within 15 days, a company spokesperson said in a statement.

None of the firm's specific compounded products are approved by the Food and Drug Administration. But Hims noted they are authorized by law and formulated by pharmacies "that adhere to rigorous quality standards and are licensed and inspected by state boards of pharmacy.".

The products include compounded formulations of sermorelin, a peptide that stimulates growth-hormone release and is marketed for recovery, body composition and anti-aging; glutathione, a peptide promoted ‌for anti-aging and athletic recovery; and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, or NAD+, a coenzyme that plays a role in cellular metabolism.

The tech giant will also offer compounded versions of vitamin B-12, a vitamin needed to make red blood cells, build DNA, and maintain healthy nerve function, and L-carnitine, an amino acid derivative that helps the body turn fat into energy. The FDA has approved certain prescription forms of both peptides for established medical uses, primarily for diagnosed deficiencies in those compounds.

Hims said it prepares to add more peptides and therapies made in the U.S. over time. That includes BPC-157, an unapproved peptide derived from a protein found in human gastric juice that is marketed for healing processes. The organization also aims to introduce another unapproved peptide called TB-500, which is derived from a naturally occurring protein in the body and is marketed for broader, systemic soft-tissue recovery and flexibility. Most of the research on both has been conducted in animals, not humans.

To receive the products, members on the Hims platform will start with an assessment of health history and goals with a licensed provider trained in peptide therapies, who can tailor a personalized plan to their needs, if appropriate.

The company stated it intends to use its communication platform to check in with patients and ensure they are seeing desired results.

It has been revealed that "If they're not, we need to do something about it," Dr. Anant Vinjamoori, Hims chief medical officer, told CNBC. "We need to, you know, adjust the dose when that's appropriate, or in some cases consider other compounds that's maybe a better fit. And of course, there will also be cases when we need to refer people to other care options.".

However, Vinjamoori noted there's still uncertainty over how to best use the peptides.

Industry observers note that "We don't have all of this data that we're used to having with compounds like this," he said. "We have the opportunity to get it right, and I think we see that as our responsibility with a organization of our size, our skill, and resources to really lead.".

Vinjamoori added that people who have serious illnesses, such as cardiovascular disease, liver disease and kidney disease, will not be candidates for the compounds for now.

Meanwhile, Andrew Huberman, a well known neuroscientist, podcaster and Stanford University School of Medicine professor who recently joined Hims' board of directors, in a statement called compounds "real medical treatments, not just a wellness trend." He remarked Hims provides safe access through "trusted sourcing and physician oversight.".

In a recent development, but health experts raised concerns about the broader mainstream marketing of peptides in the U.S. and accessing them on telehealth platforms.

"With peptides, I think you have to view them the same way you would view any drug that hasn't been rigorously tested," remarked Joshua Kritzer, a chemistry professor at Tufts University. "Without actual testing, all you have is anecdotal information, and that's just not enough information to put a substance in your body.".

Kritzer remarked the lack of large clinical trials means researchers can't rule out potentially serious, rare complications from peptides — the kinds of risks that have led regulators to reject or pull otherwise effective drugs from the market after they underwent comprehensive testing in humans.

Recent findings suggest that without that testing, it's also unclear how telehealth firms, physicians and pharmacies can make decisions about what doses patients should take, said Paul Knoepfler, a cell biology and human anatomy professor at UC Davis Health. While some people rely on anecdotal data from real peptide owners, "the dosing for these products really has not been established," he added.

Knoepfler mentioned one risk is that injecting too much of a synthetic peptide into patients could trigger "weird immune responses that are really bad for one's health" because the body might recognize it as foreign.

"With the peptides, it's very loosey-goosey," Knoepfler told CNBC. "How does one even know what would be the effective amount for whatever you're hoping it will do, and what amount would have more risks?".

But he noted the more contact patients can have with physicians around taking a compounded peptide, the better. Providers, including those tied to telehealth firms, should make sure patients are well-informed about the possible risks and unknowns of a given product and consider their preexisting conditions, cancer history and other medications, Knoepfler said.

According to recent reports, that appears to be consistent with the approach Hims & Hers is taking. The manufacturer states patients who use the peptide and longevity products can also use its Care+ offering, which pairs treatment with ongoing support. That includes twice-a-year lab testing to track their progress and the ability to message providers trained in peptide therapy around the clock with any questions.

Still, Kritzer argued that having a doctor who only knows a patient from online, essentially mail-order platforms or websites "is not enough supervision to put you on a prescription medication," especially an unapproved one.

According to recent reports, hims' ability to legally sell some of these peptides stems from a major shift in federal oversight by the Health and Human Services Department. It issued a policy in October that says the Food and Drug Administration will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or physicians that compound and dispense six unapproved peptides while formal rules are reviewed.

According to recent reports, in practice, that means these pharmacies and other firms can now offer them, even though the peptides aren't yet on the FDA's official list of ingredients compounding pharmacies are allowed to make. It does not translate to formal approval of the specific peptides.

The policy followed a 2023 decision by the Biden administration where the FDA restricted compounding pharmacies from producing popular peptide formulations due to safety, impurity and immune-reaction concerns.

HHS Secretary ​Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has supported broader access to peptides, calling himself a "substantial fan" of the treatments and arguing that restrictions were driving Americans to potentially unsafe products from overseas. Kennedy has previously described using BPC-157 to treat a muscle injury.

The announcement also comes after Hims in February 2025 acquired a California-based peptide manufacturing facility equipped with advanced peptide synthesizers.

The evidence for peptide efficacy varies by compound.

A 2026 systematic review screening 113 studies, including both small trials on humans along with rodent research, found zero eligible clinical outcome trials proving that administering IV or intramuscular NAD+ improves anti-aging, energy, or wellness endpoints in humans.

Recent findings suggest that there is some evidence for specific uses of certain peptides, such as potential weight loss. A review of 37 L-carnitine trials found participants lost about 2.7 pounds on average, though that analysis does not demonstrate that a compounded injection works the same way.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, vitamin B-12 injections are most commonly used to help people with a diagnosed deficiency rather than preventative care. U.S. survey data shows only 3.6% of adults are B-12 deficient.

Glutathione's evidence is thin, too. IV injections of it are widely marketed for skin whitening, yet not FDA-approved for this purpose.

A small study published in the Journal of Pakistan Association of Dermatologists evaluating IV glutathione highlighted that the treatment is "not very effective" for skin-lightening, and that it loses efficacy with time.

The FDA also stated in August that it received reports of at least 30 patients who experienced adverse events after they received compounded IV glutathione alone or in combination with other ingredients from different compounding pharmacies.

It has been revealed that all of the glutathione tied to the reports were from the same wholesale distributor and was labeled as dietary supplement grade, which is not an appropriate ingredient to make injectable drugs. Two of the Texas pharmacies conducted recalls related to elevated endotoxin levels in their glutathione injectable drugs.

These studies and reports don't speak to how Hims' exact combination will perform, but they do highlight the current limits on data studying the treatments and the questions surrounding them.

Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.
  • However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.
  • Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, noted an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.

However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.

Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, noted an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.

Sources indicate that he remarked a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy has claimed that North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.

Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.

However, Kovalenko added that Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future looks.

Han said it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.

It has been revealed that he told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he said, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.

Ukrainian official Kovalenko stated North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.

He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing upcoming drones and missiles.

In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy remarked that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.

According to recent reports, he warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Kovalenko remarked Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.

In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.

Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.

Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.

Ahn said that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing.

Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.

By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.

It has been revealed that kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.

Tech Report: Mysterious fresh viruses reveal a missing link in evolution

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history.
  • The research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins.
  • In a recent development, the discovery could have important implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Miami have discovered a previously unknown group of viruses that could help explain a missing piece of evolutionary history. The finding reveals an unexpected connection between viruses and tiny protein compartments inside cells, offering latest clues about how some of life's earliest biological structures may have developed.

The research, published in Nature Communications, challenges the conventional explanation for the origins of cellular structures known as encapsulins. Scientists previously believed these compartments evolved from viruses. However, the fresh evidence suggests a more complicated evolutionary relationship in which viruses and encapsulins may have repeatedly evolved from one another over millions of years.

In a recent development, the discovery could have important implications for biotechnology and for understanding the origins and early evolution of life. It also raises the possibility that viruses have biological functions that scientists have largely overlooked.

Mysterious Upcoming Viruses Reveal an Evolutionary Connection.

At the center of the discovery are proteins that fold into a distinctive three-dimensional structure known as the HK97-fold. These proteins can assemble into protective shells and are found in both viruses and encapsulins.

The newly identified viruses have smaller, simpler genomes than other viruses that produce HK97-fold protein shells. They also possess characteristics associated with both viruses and encapsulins, making them possible evolutionary intermediates between the two. Studying these unusual viruses could help researchers understand how increasingly complex biological systems first appeared.

"What makes the HK97-fold proteins so interesting is that they can form shells that enclose biochemical reactions in cellular lineages, archaea, and bacteria. But they also serve genetic purposes in viruses, storing and protecting their viral genome," said Abelardo Aguilar, the study's first author and a Ph.D. student in the Department of Biology at the University of Miami College of Arts and Sciences.

"These proteins build compartments with two different roles, which connects directly with the study of the origin of life and its early evolution because if you think about it, life at its core is about enclosing reactions and also enclosing information that can be inherited so those reactions can happen in the future.".

AI Helps Discover Hidden Viruses in Billions of DNA Sequences.

Recent findings suggest that to uncover these previously unknown viruses, Aguilar worked with Antoni Luque Santolaria, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Biology. Luque also holds secondary appointments in the Department of Physics within the College of Arts and Sciences and the Department of Chemical, Environmental and Materials Engineering in the College of Engineering. The project brought together collaborators from multiple institutions.

It has been revealed that rather than relying on laboratory experiments to grow viruses, the team searched enormous genetic databases containing billions of DNA sequences. They combined bioinformatics, models of protein behavior, and artificial intelligence tools, including protein language models and AlphaFold, to investigate the structures encoded by these sequences.

It has been revealed that the databases included IMG/M, a resource associated with the U.S. Department of Energy's Joint Genome Institute and the University of California, Berkeley. Its genetic information comes from environmental samples collected around the world, including soil, seawater, wastewater, the human gut, and numerous other locations.

This approach allows scientists to investigate viruses that have never been successfully grown in a laboratory, greatly expanding the number of organisms and evolutionary relationships they can study.

Industry observers note that "The majority of viruses cannot be grown in the lab. But now through sequencing, we have access to information on viruses for which we don't know the host, that we can't culture in the lab, but that are everywhere," Luque explained. "That means there are multiple questions in relation to evolution and how viruses have adapted to the world that it's now possible to explore bioinformatically.".

Viral Protein Shells May Have Unexpected Functions.

Beyond identifying the newly introduced viruses, the researchers proposed a possible molecular explanation for how viruses and encapsulins could have evolved from one another.

Their model centers on procapsids, immature viral protein shells (capsids) that may provide a pathway between the two types of structures. These shells could potentially support both genetic functions, such as containing viral DNA, and metabolic functions involving chemical reactions.

This raises an intriguing possibility. Viral capsids are generally recognized for packaging and protecting genetic material, but certain forms might also help create environments where biochemical reactions can occur.

"One implication of this research is the possibility that viral capsids could also facilitate biochemical reactions, which would open up the potential roles that capsids have in environments as a whole," Aguilar explained.

Although further research is needed to establish these potential functions, the findings suggest that scientists may need to look beyond the infectious stages of viruses to fully understand their roles in nature.

"When we're looking at viruses, we tend to look only at the particles that are infective, and this study points out that we might need to start putting more emphasis on the non-infective versions of the virus and what other functions those viral-like particles may have that we have overlooked in the past.".

Fresh AI Tools Open the Door to More Viral Discoveries.

In a recent development, the research also demonstrates how artificial intelligence and computational biology are transforming the study of viruses. By combining powerful analytical tools with knowledge of protein structure and physical behavior, scientists can now investigate evolutionary questions that were previously difficult to explore.

Supported by the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation and the U.S. National Science Foundation, the project provides a framework for studying other poorly understood viruses and their biological capabilities.

The researchers believe these methods could also be useful beyond evolutionary biology, including efforts to understand newly emerging viruses and pathogens.

Industry observers note that "If you have the right question and you pair it with the right tools and physical insights, it gives researchers an opportunity to look at viruses in a way that we didn't have an opportunity to do before," Luque stated. "There are evolution questions, but there are also questions about emerging pathogens or emerging viruses. The set of tools that we use can be moved forward in different contexts.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data showed with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo said in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

Recent findings suggest that “We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister said in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive upcoming leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has remarked he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

  • The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

It has been revealed that the production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as promptly as possible.

It has been revealed that "If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke noted Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

Industry observers note that the U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Recent findings suggest that ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial aims of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has stated the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.
